COLREG (Collision Regulations), denizde: COLREG (Collision Regulations) is a set of international rules that all ships must comply with in order to prevent collisions at sea.
COLREG (Convention on the International: COLREG (Convention on the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972) is an international convention prepared within IMO and entered into force in 1977 to prevent collisions, which are the most destructive type of maritime accidents. COLREG, consisting of 38 rules and annexes, is valid in all waters, including offshore and harbor entrance channels; Without prejudice to the jurisdiction of countries that have rules specific to inland water only. The rules are built on three pillars: constant and effective lookout (Rule 5), safe speed determined by the conditions (Rule 6) and the risk of conflict identified and managed at an early stage (Rules 7–8). All these technical rules are complemented by the 'good maritime practice' general provision of Rule 2: if strict adherence to the rules in unusual circumstances creates danger, the captain may take the initiative. For maritime students, COLREG is the basic legal framework that governs daily situations in both examination and real sea life.

The ship, which is stationary but whose machinery is running, emits two long blasts in succession. Sailing and fishing vessels that do not steer, have limited maneuverability, and have limited draft due to their draft, give one long and two short blasts. The towed ship (if present) gives one long and three short blasts immediately after the towing ship. A rapid bell rings at the bow of the ship at anchor (5 seconds, once a minute); On ships longer than 100 m, a gong is additionally sounded at the stern. Giving these signs correctly and on time is mandatory for both safety and legal liability.

The ship at anchor rings a bell every minute. It is a legal obligation to initiate sound signals on time. Additionally, all navigation lights are turned on, AIS status is checked, and warning messages can be broadcast.

The marine equivalent of lanes and traffic lights on the highway; navigation lights, shapes, sound signals and maneuver rules. The basic principle of the convention is that every sailor should be able to put maritime custom and common sense ahead of the rules: Rule 2 states that the rules can never be applied so rigidly as to lead to a conflict, and that even departures from the rules when necessary are legitimate to prevent conflict. Therefore, COLREG is the discipline of evaluating the situation rather than being 41 items to be memorized.

Section B's maneuverability hierarchy is critical: ships restricted in manoeuvrability (RAM), vessels restricted in shallow water (CBD), fishing vessels, sailing vessels and motor ships are ranked, with the motor ship at the bottom of the hierarchy. Knowing this hierarchy is a prerequisite for correctly determining who has the obligation to give way.
COLREG'in giriş bölümü, kuralların nasıl: The preamble of COLREG sets out how the rules are to be interpreted. Rule 1 outlines its scope of application: the high seas and all waters connected thereto in which marine vessels navigate. Rule 2 (liability) is the soul of the contract: no rule exempts the ship, master or crew from the consequences of neglecting the rules; Moreover, when special circumstances require it (imminent danger, narrow water, restricted maneuvering) it is even legitimate to deviate from the rules to avoid a conflict. This transforms COLREG from a list to be blindly memorized into a maritime discipline based on situational assessment. Rule 3 defines the terms used throughout the contract (power-propelled ship, sailboat, ship with limited manoeuvrability, ship not under command, sight of each other, restricted view); These definitions are key to the correct application of subsequent rules.

Crossing (kesişme) durumu, COLREG'in en: The crossing situation is one of the most frequently encountered and also one of the most misinterpreted scenarios of COLREG. If two motor ships are cutting each other's route at the same time in a way that creates a risk of collision and this situation does not fall within the scope of head-on or overtaking, Rule 15 comes into play. Crossing figures prominently in maritime accident statistics worldwide: incorrect ship assignment (which is the 'give-way'), late or inadequate maneuvering and miscommunication over VHF are major sources of error. For maritime faculty students, understanding the crossing scenario with its geometric, legal and operational dimensions is one of the most critical competencies in STCW exams and real sea life.

The combination of fixed bearing + decreasing range indicates the risk of conflict. Calculating the close passage point (CPA) and TCPA of the other ship with the relative vector on the ARPA is the most accurate way to determine the time required for the give-way maneuver. In practice, it is standard to take action when TCPA > 15 minutes; Leaving it later may force the stand-on ship to perform a Rule 17(b) manoeuvre. It is sometimes difficult to determine which ship is 'starboard' in the rule: if two ships are on almost the same course and intersect at a small angle difference, the head-on–crossing distinction can create a gray zone.

CSS Code, denizin asla durağan olmadığı: CSS Code arises from the fact that the sea is never static. The ship lurches, shakes fore and aft, and is thrown around; These movements impose an inertial force on the cargo that is multiples of the ship's own weight. An inadequately secured load will slip, tip over or fall overboard; this could be both fatal to the crew and devastating to the stability of the ship. The code establishes general principles and calculation methods for safe stacking and lashing of cargo. Each ship must carry and implement a Cargo Securing Manual (CSM) specific to its type and the types of cargo it carries.

CSS Code'un Ek 13 hesaplama yöntemi, gem: The Annex 13 calculation method of the CSS Code is based on numerically estimating the inertial force that ship motion exerts on the load. When the ship rolls and pitches at sea, every point on the deck is subjected to an angular acceleration and a corresponding linear acceleration; This acceleration is multiplied by the weight of the load at that point to obtain horizontal and vertical inertia forces, and the net force trying to shift or topple the load is calculated in this way. The most critical parameter of the calculation is the ship's metacentric height (GM): a ship with a high GM behaves 'stiff', that is, completes the roll quickly and with large angular acceleration, which magnifies the inertial forces on the deck load; A 'soft' (tender) ship with low GM will be slower and roll more widely, the acceleration will be smaller, but excessively low GM is dangerous for stability. Therefore, lashing design has to take into account the GM range of the ship in expected loading situations; The same load and the same lashing arrangement may have different safety margins at different GM values. Annex 13 formulates this relationship with standard motion coefficients and design wave conditions to produce the required minimum mooring capacity for each load position.
CSS uyumu kâğıt üstünde bitmez; yükleme: CSS compliance doesn't end on paper; During loading, the mooring arrangement is matched with the CSM, documented with photographs and checked periodically throughout the journey, especially in bad weather. Additional mooring precautions are taken when heavy weather is expected. Fastening heavy and project loads requires special analysis and class approval. Lashing failure is not only a safety issue but a commercial and legal risk: cargo slippage leads to PSC retention, cargo damage P&I liability and compensation claims. The code mandates this discipline for every type of cargo, from Ro-Ro vehicles to container stacks.

Cumulonimbus, tabanı deniz seviyesine ya: Cumulonimbus is a giant convective cloud whose base is close to sea level and whose top can reach the tropopause (12 km and above); Its top becomes flattened by icing and takes the characteristic anvil shape. It is the most dangerous cloud a sailor can encounter and can single-handedly produce the full range of severe weather events: thunder and lightning, sudden torrential downpours, hail, gusts that can exceed 50 knots, microbursts (downbursts) and tornadoes/waterspouts. The most critical danger is the gust front: cold downdraft within the Cb hits the surface and spreads, creating a sudden wind shift and intensification 10–15 miles ahead of the cloud, before precipitation begins. D-2 standardını karşılayan bir Balast Su: A Ballast Water Treatment System that meets the D-2 standard operates not as a single device, but as a production line consisting of complementary stages. The first stage is usually a mechanical filtration unit; While ballast is being removed, it separates large particles, sediment and macroscopic organisms from the water through a washable sieve, thus reducing the treatment load and increasing the efficiency of the next stage. The second stage is disinfection and is implemented through one of three main technologies: UV radiation disrupts cell DNA, preventing organisms from multiplying; Electrochlorination disinfects the salt in seawater by converting it to sodium hypochlorite by electrolysis and producing active chlorine; Ozonation breaks down the cell structure with ozone gas, which is a strong oxidant. Before discharge, usually a neutralization step (in chlorine-based systems) reduces the residual oxidant level below the discharge limit. To prove that the system actually delivers D-2 performance after installation, commissioning testing is carried out: an independent sampling team samples the intake and discharge waters during the actual ballast operation and validates the viable organism count (for size classes >50 μm and 10-50 μm) and bacterial indicators in the laboratory. Without passing this test, the certificate is not issued and the system is not considered D-2 compliant.
D-2 standardını sağlamak için balast suy: Ballast water treatment systems are used to meet the D-2 standard. Common technologies: filtration + killing/inactivating organisms with ultraviolet (UV); filtration + electrochlorination/chemical disinfection (active substance). The system is activated during ballast intake and/or discharge. Sediments (sludge containing organisms that accumulate at the bottom of the tank) are regularly managed and disposed of appropriately. Correct operation and calibration of the BWMS is critical to ensure that discharge remains within legal limits.

Demirin tutması, yeterli kaloma (salınan: The anchor holds when sufficient scope (paid-out chain length / water depth ratio) is given. Denetimde bulunan her eksiklik standart: Each deficiency found during the inspection is recorded with standard codes and an action is assigned: some are corrected on site, some are postponed to the next port or for a certain period of time. The most severe consequence is detention: the ship is detained from sailing until serious deficiencies are corrected and suffers commercial losses during this period. Repeated detentions may lead to a regional ban on the ship. The consequences are not limited to single ships: detentions affect the flag state's White/Grey/Black list ranking, which determines the inspection frequency of all ships of that flag. That's why ships carry out internal inspection (pre-PSC) before entering the port and close the deficiencies in advance.
Denetimde bulunan her eksiklik, standart: Each deficiency found in the audit is recorded with a standardized code and a corrective action is assigned to it. Some deficiencies are corrected on the spot (code 10), some are postponed to be corrected at the next port (code 15) or within a certain period of time (code 16, e.g. 14 days), some are notified to the flag state or classification society (code 17/45). The most severe action is detention (code 30): the ship cannot leave the port until serious deficiencies have been corrected and it is safe. Deficiencies are grouped into 17 main categories (certificates, structural safety, fire safety, lifesaving, navigational safety, MARPOL, ISM, ISPS, MLC, BWM, etc.) and contain hundreds of subcodes. This standardization ensures that auditors in every port of the world speak the same language and that results are shared consistently in regional databases (THETIS, APCIS).

Designated Person Ashore (DPA), ISM Code: Designated Person Ashore (DPA) is the ISM Code's most unique corporate innovation: it aims to establish a direct, unfiltered line of communication between the ship and the company's top management. What the rule clearly requires is that the DPA has direct access to the highest level of management of the company; This means the DPA is not trapped within the hierarchy of operational or commercial departments, nor dependent on the approval of a supervisor with a commercial or operational conflict of interest when reporting a safety concern. The logic behind this access requirement is clear: when a captain reports a safety risk, this information should not be filtered internally and mitigated by commercial considerations such as 'not delaying the voyage' or 'not increasing cost'. The role of the DPA in daily practice is largely proactive rather than reactive: it monitors internal audit results, analyzes near-miss and non-conformity reports, conveys concerns from the ship to senior management and, when necessary, defends the company's resource allocation decisions (personnel, maintenance budget, equipment renewal) in line with safety requirements. When this independence of the DPA is weakened, ISM auditors often identify this as the system's most vulnerable point.

DMLC (Declaration of Maritime Labour Com: DMLC (Declaration of Maritime Labor Compliance) is the original and practical heart of the MLC 2006 certification system. The MLC Certificate 'certifies' compliance but does not explain how it is achieved; DMLC fills this gap and is kept on board as an integral annex to the certificate. It is in two parts: Part I is prepared by the flag state and explains what national legislation requires in the 14 MLC areas (with national equivalent differences, if any); The company prepares Part II and puts forward the implementation plan showing how it actually meets these requirements in each area. Thus, the statement answers both the questions 'what the rule says' and 'how do we apply it' in a single document.
DMLC denetiminin en kritik yönü, Part II: The most critical aspect of the DMLC audit is to compare whether each procedure written in Part II has actually been implemented on the ship. The most serious risk is inconsistency between declaration and reality: for example, if Part II says working hours are recorded but the records are incomplete, or if a grievance mechanism is defined but the crew is unaware of this, this is a major discrepancy and possible cause for detention. Therefore, Part II should be updated and reported to the flag state/RO whenever the company's personnel policy or procedures change; Changes to national requirements in Part I should be monitored; Concrete evidence of compliance (records, contracts, certificates) for each of the 14 areas should be kept available on board. DMLC makes sense together with MLC Certificate; If the certificate is invalid, the DMLC also becomes invalid and the ship cannot sail internationally.

Part I explains what the flag state requires in each area (and national equivalent differences, if any); Part II lays out the implementation plan that shows how the company actually meets these requirements. Dökme tahılın kayma tehlikesi, katı bir: The danger of bulk grain slipping arises from a peculiar mechanical property of a solid pile, the angle of repose: friction between the grains allows the pile to maintain its shape up to a certain angle of inclination, but once this angle is exceeded the grains slide over each other, creating a new, lower equilibrium surface. When grain is loaded onto the ship, it forms a surface close to the hold ceiling, but vibration and shaking during the voyage reduce the space between the grains, causing the cargo to 'settle'; this seating leaves a gap at the top. When the ship rolls, this gap expands towards the inclined side, and the grain mass slides into this gap when it encounters a slope exceeding its comfortable angle. The sliding mass shifts the center of gravity of the ship towards the direction of heel, which causes the ship to take a permanent heel to that side, that is, the righting moment decreases. This is the importance of the practical limit of 12°: a permanent heel below this angle is considered controllable while the ship still has sufficient reserves of freeboard and righting moment; Above this limit, the subsequent wave or wind roll enters a region where the ship exhausts its righting moment and approaches capsize.
Dökme tehlikeli maddelerde kayma potansi: In bulk hazardous materials, risks such as slip potential, moisture sensitivity, self-heating and gas formation indirectly affect stability. Extinguishing water pumped into the hold creates a large free surface effect and rapidly reduces GM.

Dökme yük gemileri, denizdeki en yüksek: Bulk carriers have been one of the ship types with the highest loss rate at sea. The pattern seen in Derbyshire and similar losses was frightening: ships sank very quickly, often without even being able to issue a distress call. The reason was that heavy and dense loads strained the warehouse structure, and water intake in a warehouse quickly led to structural collapse and sinking. These losses led to the addition of SOLAS Chapter XII and the introduction of additional structural and operational requirements specific to bulk carriers. The BC Code and subsequent regulations impose strict rules on both the structural strength and loading operations of these ships.
Dökme yük gemileri, gemi tipleri arasınd: Bulk carriers have long ranked among the worst in total loss statistics among ship types, and this is not due to a single mistake, but to the overlapping of multiple risks. The first mechanism is the single hold flood scenario: dense loads such as ore or coal are piled up in a narrow volume on the warehouse floor, which subjects the warehouse structure (especially the slanting plates between the side tanks and the hold) to heavy static and dynamic loads; When a corrosion or fatigue crack in a hold's hull plate grows rapidly and allows it to take on water, the ship often goes upside down within minutes, leaving the crew with no chance to evacuate. The second mechanism is structural fatigue: repeated loading-unloading cycles create cumulative stress fluctuations in the hull, which in neglected ships develop into fatigue cracks. The third and relatively more recently recognized mechanism is liquefaction: moist fine-grained cargoes such as nickel ore, when vibrated by ship motion, can lose their solid appearance and suddenly behave like a liquid, causing the ship to overturn due to the free surface effect. The emergence of these three mechanisms in successive disasters forced IMO to adopt SOLAS Chapter XII and introduce structural strength, water level alert and post-damage survival requirements specific to bulk carriers.

Dördüncü Zabit (Fourth Officer / Junior: Fourth Officer (Junior Officer) is the most junior watch officer who learns and practices independent navigational watchkeeping on the bridge under the supervision of the Captain or First Officer. This shift is usually carried out in the 00-04 (graveyard watch) and 12-16 hours. This section; As an OOW (Officer of the Watch), it explains step by step the use of radar/ECDIS/ARPA, COLREG application, position verification, logbook keeping and shift handover procedures from the perspective of a junior officer and within the framework of surveillance. Its purpose is to balance independent shift preparation with supervised responsibility.
Dördüncü Zabit, gemi limanda yatarken gü: The Fourth Officer is the officer of the watch who is responsible for the security of the ship by keeping a gangway watch while the ship is lying in the harbour, supervision of entry and exit from the ship, and deck supervision during cargo operations. This seizure; Enforcement of ISPS security level requirements includes visitor and crew registration, mooring and draft monitoring, fire/pollution surveillance and emergency preparedness. A port watch is conducted in a static environment, unlike a navigational watch at sea; However, it requires at least as much attention in terms of safety, security and environmental risks. This section describes the gangway watch's scope of duty and procedures from the junior officer perspective.
Dördüncü Zabit, güverte departmanının en: The Fourth Officer is the most junior officer in the deck department and is not required to be present on every ship; However, he undertakes bridge watch, safety equipment checks and support to cargo operations on the ships he is on. It is a critical period for completing the training process and gaining experience. Must have the necessary competency certificate to keep independent shifts within the scope of STCW.
Dördüncü Zabit, İkinci Zabit'in (Navigat: The Fourth Officer contributes to keeping the ship's navigational information up to date and also learns this critical administrative task by providing supervised support to the chart and navigational broadcast management under the responsibility of the Second Officer. This support; It covers Notices to Mariners (NtM) tracking, paper chart and ECDIS corrections, T&P (Temporary & Preliminary) Notice processing, preparation of folio lists and keeping the publication inventory up to date. SOLAS V/27 makes it a legal obligation for ships' charts and publications to be up to date. This chapter explains step by step the methodology of chart-broadcast maintenance from the junior officer perspective.
Dördüncü Zabit, kariyerinin başında köpr: At the beginning of his career, the Fourth Officer establishes his professional foundation by learning bridge devices, safety and operation procedures and deck maintenance systems. Use of devices such as ECDIS, radar, AIS, GMDSS; Management systems such as ISM, ISPS, SOPEP; Load operation procedures and Training Record Book discipline are internalized during this period. This chapter deals with the structured way in which the junior officer learns systems and procedures.
Dördüncü Zabit, liman ve demir operasyon: The Fourth Officer actively supports the execution of cargo operations under the coordination of the First Officer (Chief Officer / Cargo Officer) in port and anchor operations. This task; It includes loading/unloading supervision, tank and hold sounds, draft reading, cargo tally holding, hatch cover opening/closing and lashing/securing controls. In these operations, the junior officer is both physically present on deck and prepares to be a cargo officer by monitoring the First Officer's cargo plan and stowage calculations. This chapter establishes the step-by-step foundation of the ability to conduct independent freight operation with supervised responsibility.
Dördüncü Zabit, Üçüncü Zabit'in (genelli: The Fourth Officer, under the supervision of the Third Officer (usually the Safety Officer on board), supports periodic checks of life-saving (LSA - Life-Saving Appliances) and fire-fighting equipment (FFE - Fire-Fighting Equipment). This task; It covers lifejacket and lifebuoy counting/control, fire cabinets and hoses, portable fire extinguishers, muster list applications and drill preparations. This section provides practical guidance for the junior officer to inspect safety equipment in accordance with legislation, keep records and report deficiencies.

Fuel consumption can significantly change the position of the ship's center of gravity; KG may increase or decrease, especially depending on the location of the fuel tanks. For this reason, the arrival state must also meet the stability criteria independently.
durumu, geminin kargo olmaksızın yalnızc: this is the scenario where the ship sails with only ballast water and no cargo. Having full ballast tanks ensures adequate propeller sinking and bow draft remains at acceptable levels. In the case of ballast, the displacement is low and the wind surface area of the ship is large; Therefore, the wind heeling moment becomes more critical. Since the KM value differs at low displacements, separate stability evaluation is mandatory for ballast cases.
durumu, geminin maksimum kargo kapasites: this is the scenario where the ship leaves the port at maximum cargo capacity, with 100% fuel and fresh water and all consumables fully loaded. This generally corresponds to the highest displacement and creates a critical scenario for stability as the VCG (vertical center of gravity) potential is highest. In case of full load departure, draft and trim values must not exceed the loadline limits and all IMO stability criteria must be met.
durumu, uzun bir balast seyiri sonrasınd: this is the scenario in which the destination port is reached with minimum fuel after a long ballast cruise. ECDIS (Electronic Chart Display and Info: Navigation with ECDIS (Electronic Chart Display and Information System) is only safe if the charts and data are kept up to date. As the navigating officer, the Second Officer is responsible for keeping the official ENC service subscription up to date, uploading weekly updates, processing T&P (Temporary & Preliminary) notes and keeping the ECDIS backup system operational. This section covers the ECDIS update cycle, T&P management, and audit records.

ECDIS (Electronic Chart Display and Information System) is an advanced bridge navigation system that integrates electronic navigational charts (ENC - Electronic Navigational Chart) with ship sensor data, which can officially replace the paper chart, provided that it meets IMO standards. It became mandatory gradually between 2012 and 2018 with the SOLAS Part V regulation; Passenger ships of 10,000 GT and above and commercial ships of 3000 GT and above must carry ECDIS.

The main value of ECDIS lies in its continuous and automatic comparison between geographical location (GPS/GNSS) and map hazards. The system generates an alarm when the ship approaches a dangerous area. However, this power also leads to a dangerous trap called 'automation reliance': the navigator's over-reliance on ECDIS and the relegation of manual verification and independent thought. Many maritime accidents in recent years have been caused by procedural errors in the use of ECDIS.

ECDIS (Electronic Chart Display and Information System) is an electronic navigation system that is considered the legal equivalent of a paper map. It must comply with IMO MSC.232(82) performance standards.

ECDIS (Electronic Chart Display and Information System) is a system that is the legal equivalent of a paper chart, providing cruise planning and tracking by combining approved electronic navigation charts (ENC) with location, radar/AIS and sensor data. SOLAS has made it mandatory for most commercial ships to carry ECDIS. This section; It discusses in depth the difference between ENC and RNC, system architecture and sensor inputs, route planning/control (safety contour, guard zone) functions, alarm management, update and backup requirements and common usage errors.

EEXI is the existing fleet-adapted sibling of EEDI, which is mandatory for new ships: EEDI is calculated once when the ship is designed, while EEXI is applied as a one-time threshold to ships already at sea. As they both measure design (technical) efficiency, they should be considered alongside the CII, which measures the annual operational performance of the ship: EEXI answers the question 'how efficiently the ship is designed', while CII answers the question 'how efficiently the ship is actually operated'. If compliance is not achieved, the IAPP certificate will not be renewed and the ship will not be able to sail internationally.

EEXI'nin temelinde, geminin teorik karbo: The basis of EEXI is a formula that measures the theoretical carbon efficiency of the ship: the denominator is the total CO₂ emissions based on the power of the main and auxiliary engines, their specific fuel consumption and the carbon factor of the fuel; The denominator represents the product of the ship's carrying capacity (DWT or GT) and the reference speed (Vref). The result is the 'achieved EEXI' in gCO₂/tonne·miles and must not exceed the 'required EEXI' reference line determined by ship type and size; this baseline is based on the reduction factors in the EEDI phases. Various correction factors go into the calculation: factors such as capacity correction (fi), cubic capacity correction (fc) and ice class/weather condition. EEXI is a fixed one-time threshold that evaluates the theoretical efficiency of the ship's design, not its actual navigational data.

In the cargo area, ODME (Oil Discharge Monitoring Equipment), which monitors the cargo oil discharge for tankers, slop tank arrangement that collects dirty washing water, and Crude Oil Washing (COW) systems, which reduce the residue by washing the tank with its own cargo in crude oil tankers, are envisaged. Separated ballast tanks (SBT) prevent ballast water from coming into contact with oil. The double hull structure, which became mandatory after the 1990s, reduces the risk of rupture of the cargo tank in collisions and groundings. The proliferation of electronic navigation systems has required the bridge to manage multiple digital information streams. Cross-checking is based on the principle of verifying each source by comparing location and environmental information obtained from different and independent sources. This principle directly addresses the danger of blind reliance on a single sensor and is essential to meet COLREG's obligation of appropriate stewardship.

SOLAS Chapter V Regulation 19 requires the use of suitable means of navigation and verification of their reliability. The discipline of cross-checking allows the navigator to recognize system errors and GPS/ECDIS anomalies before they become real dangers.

EPIRB (Emergency Position Indicating Rad: EPIRB (Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon) and SART (Search and Rescue Transponder) are critical devices for locating and directing rescue units in case of abandonment of the ship or severe emergency situations. The correct operation of these devices directly determines the life-saving time in a real emergency. Testing, maintenance and recording discipline is as important as the physical existence of the device.

EPIRB (Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon) is a beacon device that transmits the ship's MMSI and GPS position to Cospas-Sarsat satellites on the 406 MHz frequency, automatically or manually activated when the ship is abandoned. On SOLAS ships, it is mounted outside the bridge, in a quick access bracket, with a hydrostatic release unit (HRU).

It is released at a certain depth with hydrostatic release (HRU) and is automatically activated with water. This section; It covers EPIRB operation and Cospas-Sarsat satellite system, 406 MHz digital identity and GPS location, float-free and HRU mechanism, registration and false alarm management, SOLAS requirement and maintenance/malfunction in engineering depth.

ESP sörveylerinin biriken sonuçları, bir: The accumulated results of ESP surveys determine not only the current class status of a ship but also its long-term economic future. Thickness measurement trends follow a degradation curve over the years; This curve allows predicting when certain structural elements will approach the minimum thickness limit, thus when and to what extent steel renewal will be required. At this point, the shipowner makes a basic economic decision: is it still profitable considering the impending major steel refurbishment expense, the remaining commercial life of the ship and the scrap/second-hand ship prices at the time, or is it more rational to send the ship for dismantling? This calculation is made frequently, especially in bulk carriers and tankers over 15-20 years old; The finding of widespread 'substantial corrosion' revealed in an ESP survey is not an issue that can be solved with a single repair, but may be a signal indicating the end of the economic life of the ship. Therefore, the ESP file is not just an audit trail, it is a basic data set that fleet management uses in asset lifecycle planning.
ESP'nin kapsamı rastgele seçilmemiştir;: The scope of ESP was not chosen randomly; Bulk carriers and tankers are the two ship types where structural failure is most common in ship loss statistics, and there are concrete engineering reasons for this. In bulk carriers, holds are exposed to local stress concentrations created by repeated loading-unloading cycles of high-density solid cargo (mine, coal, grain) and mechanical damage caused by equipment such as grabs/excavators; This accelerates fatigue cracks, especially at hatch bottom corners and transverse bulkheads. In tankers, the problem is chemical: water, hydrogen sulfide and other corrosive components contained in crude oil and its derivatives cause rapid and sometimes unpredictable corrosion, especially on ballast tank upper surfaces and cargo tank steel structures. In both cases, damage accumulates in closed volumes that are invisible to an outside observer and can reach critical levels without warning. Successive bulk carrier losses in the 1990s demonstrated that existing general class surveys were inadequate to capture this type of structural risk, prompting IACS to develop a more frequent and in-depth survey regime specific to these two ship types.
ESP'nin teknik kalbi, geminin çeliğinin: The technical heart of ESP is monitoring how thin the ship's steel becomes over time. Ultrasonic thickness measurement (UTM) is systematically performed in critical structural regions and each measurement is evaluated as part of a trend; When the 'significant' and 'substantial corrosion' thresholds are exceeded, repair or reinforcement becomes necessary. Close-up survey requires the surveyor to physically reach the structural elements inside the tank via scaffolding or rafting (staging/rafting) and closely examine cracks and deformations. The condition of the tank coating and cathodic protection is also evaluated, as coating degradation is a sign of corrosion.
ESP'yi tek seferlik bir denetimden ayıra: What distinguishes ESP from a one-off inspection is that it retains a lifetime structural memory of the ship. ESP file, which must be kept on board; It houses all past survey records, thickness measurement trends and repair history. In this way, the surveyor can make decisions for the future by seeing the rate of deterioration over the years, not the current condition of the ship. The survey scope is planned according to the age and type of the ship; Cleaning and gas-free operations (with closed space entry rules) are required for safe inspection of tanks. Failure to file an ESP on time will result in class suspension, while incomplete filing will result in a PSC finding.

EU ETS denizcilikte kademeli devreye gir: EU ETS phases in for shipping: obligation covers 40% of emissions in 2024, 70% in 2025, 100% from 2026; also, after 2026, methane and nitrous oxide are included in addition to CO₂. The geographical coverage is fine-tuned: the entire emissions of voyages between two EU ports, half of the voyages between an EU port and a non-EU port, the entire time spent at anchor in an EU port are covered. This design aims to limit carbon leakage without exceeding the EU's jurisdiction. Each ship takes as its 'managing authority' the EU state it has visited most in recent years.
EU ETS hangi gemiler ve seferler için em: For which ships and voyages does the EU ETS require emission rights?
EU ETS maliyeti sefer planlamasını ve ya: EU ETS cost directly affects voyage planning and fuel selection.
EU ETS yıllık bir takvimle işler: yıl bo: The EU ETS operates on an annual schedule: emissions are monitored throughout the year, a certified emissions report is submitted to an independent verifier by 31 March of the following year, and a sufficient number of EUAs are submitted by 30 September. The cost of these obligations is important and charter contracts must clearly state who will pay (shipowner or charterer). Sanctions are harsh: a penalty is paid for each tonne underdelivered, and the quota delivery obligation still remains; Non-compliance lasting more than two years may result in the ship being banned from EU ports (expulsion order). EU ETS, together with FuelEU Maritime in the same scope, constitutes the 'Fit for 55' maritime leg of the EU.
EU ETS, denizciliğe getirilen ilk büyük: The EU ETS is the first major carbon pricing system introduced to shipping and is unique in that it is a non-IMO, regional EU regulation. Its logic is based on the 'polluter pays' principle: a ship must purchase and deliver a market-traded emissions quota (EUA) for every tonne of CO₂ it produces within the EU. Thus, carbon emission is no longer free, but turns into a cost item with a price, and the ship operator is encouraged to avoid this cost by reducing emissions. The system is built on the EU MRV infrastructure, which has been collecting data since 2018.

Execution (Uygulama), planlanan seyrin f:
Execution is the third phase in which the planned course is actually carried out. This phase lasts from departure to arrival and is the process in which the plan is compared with real-world conditions, compatibility problems are resolved and dynamic decisions are made. The success of the execution is directly proportional to the quality of the plan and the BRM (Bridge Resource Management) skill of the bridge team.

Execution is not passive following a plan; It is a process based on active, critical and situational awareness. Each officer of the watch must evaluate whether the plan made at take-off is still valid, whether conditions are compatible with the plan and, if necessary, the extent to which changes are required.

Eyewall (göz duvarı), gözü çepeçevre sar: Eyewall is the ring consisting of vertically developed cumulonimbus clouds up to 8–15 km high, surrounding the eye and is arguably the most dangerous region of the tropical cyclone. The system's highest sustained winds, strongest gusts, heaviest precipitation, and steepest pressure gradient are found here. Wind speed can jump from near zero to over 100 knots within a few knots as it passes from the calm center of the eye to the eyewall; There is no such sharp transition in any other meteorological system. The barometer can rise or fall at extraordinary rates of 15–20 hPa per hour during eyewall passage. In the Northern Hemisphere, the strongest wind is generally located in the right-front quadrant of the eyewall (relative to the direction of motion of the system); because here the progress speed of the system is added to the rotational wind of the cyclone — this is the micro-scale equivalent of the dangerous semicircle concept. The sea state below the eyewall is beyond definable limits: chaotic waves exceeding 15 meters, visibility reduced to zero due to drifting spray, and the highest values of storm surge in coastal areas are produced in the eyewall region. No commercial ship can maneuver safely in eyewall conditions; The goal of the entire evasion strategy is to keep the ship as far away from this ring as possible.

Eyewall'dan dışa doğru, sistemin dönüş y: Spiral rain bands extend outward from the eyewall, spiraling towards the center in the direction of rotation of the system. Each band; It is like a convective line that carries heavy rain, sudden wind increases (squall), thunderstorms and occasional waterspout/tornado activity. The bands appear on the radar screen as bright arcs bending towards the center, and an experienced observer can roughly estimate the bearing of the cyclone center from the curvature of the bands. In the corridors between the bands, precipitation eases, winds become relatively regulated, and the sky may partially clear; These intervals can create the illusion that the storm is passing amid worsening conditions. However, as the ship approaches the center, the bands become more frequent, the intervals become shorter, and each new band becomes more intense than the previous one. Since wind direction and speed can change within minutes during band crossings, deck operations should not be planned relying on these deceptively calm intervals. In the outermost periphery of the system, high clouds (cirus shield), gradually growing long-period faints and a regular decrease in pressure disrupting the daily tidal oscillation (diurnal variation) are observed; These are classic early signs that a cyclone is approaching while the center is still hundreds of miles away.

FAL Sözleşmesi, bir geminin limanla etki: The FAL Convention standardizes the entire administrative process of a ship's interaction with the port. Before arrival, the ship transmits cargo, crew, dangerous goods and health status information via pre-arrival notification; This allows port and border authorities to prepare in advance. The information that customs, immigration, health and port authorities may request during your stay in the port is limited to the maximum set of documents allowed by the contract; The contract aims to prevent public authorities from requesting unnecessary or repetitive documents. Similarly, formalities are minimized on departure. The main tool of this standardization is the globally recognized FAL forms (General Declaration, Cargo, Stores, Crew Baggage, Crew and Passenger lists, Dangerous Cargo Manifesto); The same data does not have to be prepared again in a different format at each port.
FAL Sözleşmesi, emniyet ya da çevre deği: The FAL Convention is not about safety or the environment; It is the only IMO convention focused on efficiency. Its aim is to minimize, standardize and electronicize as much as possible the documents and formalities required for a ship's entry and exit from the port. Unnecessary paperwork and repetitive notifications both keep the ship waiting in the port and increase the cost of trade. FAL reduces this friction and streamlines international maritime trade by bringing the information that public authorities (customs, border, health, port) may request from the ship into a common form.
FAL'ın çağdaş atılımı, kâğıt formalitele: FAL's contemporary breakthrough is to move paper formalities to electronic data interchange. Maritime Single Window (MSW) ensures that all ship-related notifications are made once and shared with all relevant institutions from a single electronic entry point; This puts an end to the same information being given over and over to different departments and reduces the bureaucracy that keeps the ship waiting in port. The latest revisions also include digital certificate exchange and automation of processes. The Convention also has a humanitarian dimension: regarding stowaways, standard procedures are defined for the detection of stowaways, their accommodation on the ship in humane conditions, sharing of responsibility among flag/port/port of call states, and their repatriation. Thus, FAL observes both efficiency and humane standards while accelerating trade.
FAL'ın en köklü dönüşümü, gemi-liman ver: The most radical transformation of FAL is that it moves ship-port data exchange from paper form to an electronic single window. The Maritime Single Window requirement, adopted with the FAL 13 (2019) amendments and becoming mandatory in all state party ports from 2024, reduces the previously repeated notifications to each public authority (customs, immigration, health, port authority, security) separately and often on paper, to a data set that is entered once from a single digital interface and automatically distributed to all relevant institutions. This change isn't just about saving paper; It also eliminates the risk of inconsistency and delay that occurs when the same information is entered repeatedly in different formats by the agency, captain or owner. The technical backbone of the system is to transport data of standard FAL forms (1-7) with common data models and messaging standards (e.g. UN/EDIFACT-based or XML formatted); Thus, by uploading a single file, a shipping agency can transmit the General Declaration, Cargo Declaration, Crew and Passenger List information to all competent authorities simultaneously. For developing port authorities, this transition is a serious capacity challenge requiring infrastructure investment and staff training; IMO provides support to these countries through technical cooperation programs.
FAL'ın son yıllardaki en önemli atılımı,: FAL's most important breakthrough in recent years is the Maritime Single Window (MSW) obligation: all ship-related notifications are made once, from a single electronic entry point, and shared with all relevant institutions. This puts an end to paper forms and giving the same information over and over to different departments. The latest revisions also include digital certificate exchange and automation of processes. FAL compliance in terms of ship management; It means sending out pre-arrival notifications in a timely manner, integrating into MSW systems, and teaching crews about stowaway procedures.
FAL'ın yedi standart formu, soyut bir be: FAL's seven standard forms are not an abstract list of documents, but a workflow that corresponds exactly to the chronological flow of a port call. In the pre-notification phase before arrival, the ship agency ensures advance preparation of the port, customs and health authorities by transmitting basic information about the ship's ETA, cargo and crew (draft of the General Declaration, Cargo Declaration, Dangerous Cargo Manifesto). On arrival, the General Declaration (FAL 1) formalizes the ship's identity and navigational information, the Crew List (FAL 5) and Passenger List (FAL 6) are submitted to immigration/border control, and the Store Declaration (FAL 3) and Crew Luggage Declaration (FAL 4) are submitted to customs. Changes regarding cargo operations during the stay in port are updated in the Cargo Declaration. On departure, a subset of the documents on arrival is usually resubmitted in an updated form. Keeping the number and content of these documents to a minimum is directly reflected in port efficiency: if a ship waits at the dock or at anchor due to document processing, this means both demurrage-like costs for the shipowner and inefficient use of port capacity. Therefore, FAL's principle of 'no unnecessary or repetitive documents can be requested' is a concrete economic tool that directly shortens port turnaround time.

FSS Code çeşitli söndürme yöntemlerini f: The FSS Code regulates various extinguishing methods for different spaces: fixed CO₂ or foam systems (smothering principle) for high-risk confined spaces such as engine rooms, automatic sprinklers and water mist systems for accommodation spaces, deck foam monitors for cargo areas. In asphyxiating systems such as CO₂, audio/visual warning and time delay are mandatory for people to evacuate. On the detection side, smoke and heat detectors are arranged in zones and loops; The location of a fire can be instantly seen from the panel on the bridge. Manual alarm points initiate human intervention before the automated system catches up.
FSS Code zorunlu hale geldi – yangın güv: FSS Code becomes mandatory – standardization of fire safety systems
FSS Code, her mahallin riskine uygun sab: FSS Code links fixed extinguishing systems to detailed standards appropriate to the risks of each location. For high-risk closed spaces such as engine rooms, fixed gas systems (CO₂ and equivalent) extinguish fire by suffocating oxygen; In these systems, there is an audio/visual warning and a mandatory time delay for people to evacuate, because the gas released into the environment is suffocating for people. Foam systems seal the fuel from the air by covering the surface of the burning liquid with a film layer and are used in engine rooms and tanker decks. Water mist systems provide oxygen dilution through both cooling and evaporation with very small water droplets and have become increasingly common after the halon ban. The code defines the agent quantity, coverage rate, evacuation time, and alarm requirements for each system, along with methods for calculating them.
FSS Code, manuel müdahale araçlarını da: The FSS Code also standardizes the means of manual intervention: fire main, hydrants, hoses and fire pumps of appropriate capacity (including emergency fire pump) and portable extinguishers are available on every ship. Firefighter equipment – self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA), heat-resistant suit, helmet, gloves, lifeline and emergency escape breathing devices (EEBD) – enables the team to get close to the fire. All of these systems remain reliable only with regular testing: the annual weight check of CO₂ cylinders, the weekly function test of alarm panels, the periodic open/close test of fire doors and dampers, the pressure check of SCBA cylinders and the servicing of portable extinguishers cannot be neglected. An undercharged CO₂ system or an inoperative alarm will result in serious deficiency and retention of PSC monitoring; The FSS Code thus forms the technical guarantee of SOLAS Chapter II-2.
FSS Code, SOLAS Chapter II-2'nin 'yangın: FSS Code is SOLAS Chapter II-2's technical answer to the question 'how to fight fire'. A fire on the ship must be taken under control with the ship's resources from the first minutes, since it is impossible to get help from land; Therefore, the design, performance and availability of extinguishing, detection and alarm systems are vital. The code standardizes how each system will be sized, where it will be located, how it will be tested, and how it will be maintained. Thus, the ship's passive protection (structural fire compartments) and active protection (extinguishing systems) establish a defense that complements each other.

FuelEU katı bir yıllık limit dayatmak ye: Rather than imposing a rigid annual limit, FuelEU offers flexibility tools. With compliance balance, the improvement (surplus) made in one year can be transferred to the next year or the deficit can be borrowed. The pooling mechanism allows for exchange between ships: a very clean ship can transfer its surplus as credit to another ship that is substandard; This is a particularly powerful tool in fleet management. As a separate obligation, from 2030 container and cruise ships must use onshore power supply (OPS) when docked in EU ports, eliminating emissions and air pollution from engine operation in port. In case of default, penalties calculated on the VLSFO equivalent are applied.

FuelEU Maritime ve EU ETS aynı gemileri,: FuelEU Maritime and EU ETS target the same ships, the same voyages and largely the same emissions data, but are not interchangeable; A shipowner must comply with both regulations independently and simultaneously. While the EU ETS generates a cost per carbon because it puts a direct price on emissions, FuelEU places a technical cap on the GHG intensity of the fuel; Even if a ship obtains an EUA and meets its ETS obligation, it will face a separate deficit penalty if it exceeds the FuelEU limit. This dual structure is strategically important as a single compliance tool (e.g. using a biofuel blend) impacts both regulations simultaneously: the biofuel blend both reduces CO₂ burned (hence the need for EUA) and improves the Well-to-Wake density of the fuel (hence FuelEU compliance). So shipowners typically model the costs of the two arrangements together and try to optimize both with a single fuel strategy; A strategy that looks at only one may have an unexpected cost in the other.
FuelEU Maritime Well-to-Wake bazlıdır (y: FuelEU Maritime is Well-to-Wake based (not just stack emissions)
FuelEU Maritime, 2025'ten itibaren gemi: FuelEU Maritime sets a target to gradually reduce the GHG intensity of ship fuels from 2025.
FuelEU Maritime, EU ETS ile aynı gemiler: FuelEU Maritime targets the same ships as EU ETS but uses different leverage. While the EU ETS puts a price on emissions, FuelEU puts a direct cap on the greenhouse gas intensity of the energy used by the ship (gCO₂eq/MJ). In other words, instead of 'no matter how much you pollute', it says 'the fuel you use has to be cleaner and cleaner'. This approach forces operators to switch to lower carbon fuels (biofuel, e-fuels, green methanol/ammonia) over time. The two regulations work together: one with a price signal, the other with a standard mandate, pushing for the same decarbonisation target.
FuelEU Maritime: 2025-2050 arası kademel: FuelEU Maritime: Phased GHG reduction targets 2025-2050
FuelEU'nun en ayırt edici yönü Well-to-W: The most distinctive aspect of FuelEU is its Well-to-Wake approach: not only the emissions of the fuel when it is burned on board (Tank-to-Wake), but its entire life cycle emissions from production to transportation are taken into account. This is important because even if a fuel burns cleanly on board, a lot of carbon may have been released in its production; The WtW gaze makes this 'hidden' emission visible. Permissible GHG concentrations gradually tighten from 2025 to 2050 (starting at 2% to 80% reduction). The use of renewable e-fuels (RFNBO) is rewarded with multiplier bonuses, and wind-assisted propulsion systems are also rewarded with benefits.
FuelEU'nun limiti sefer bazlı değil, gem: FuelEU's limit is calculated not on a voyage basis, but on the energy-weighted average of all the energy the ship uses during the calendar year. That is, if the ship used different fuel types (VLSFO, LNG, biofuel blend) in a year, the share of each fuel in the total energy consumption is multiplied by the Well-to-Wake GHG intensity value of that fuel and all contributions are summed to obtain a single average gCO₂eq/MJ value of the ship for that year. This average is compared to the current limit for that year. The practical result of this method is that using clean fuel in one go alone is not enough, what really matters is the total weight of the fuel mixture throughout the year; A ship cannot try to meet the limit by using conventional fuel for most of the year and burning biofuel for a short period at the end of the year, because the low volume clean fuel share will not reduce the annual average sufficiently. Gelgit (tide), Ay ve Güneş’in yerçekimse:
Tide is the periodic rise and fall of the water level in the oceans and seas due to the gravitational influence of the Moon and the Sun. This effect is astronomically predictable, so tide tables can be calculated long periods in advance. The tide shows different characters around the world: in some ports it rises and falls twice a day (semidiurnal), in others it rises and falls twice a day (diurnal), and in others a mixed cycle is observed.

The importance of tide in terms of maritime is multifaceted: tide information plays a critical role in areas such as port entry-exit timing, UKC (Under Keel Clearance) calculation, under-bridge passage height, coastal passage safety and water surface estimation in rescue operations. Gelgit tabloları (tidal tables), belirli:
Tidal tables give each day's High Water (HW) and Low Water (LW) times and heights for a particular reference port (standard port), usually in UT (UTC) and in meters relative to the chart datum. Admiralty Tide Tables (ATT), publications of the Department of Navigation, Hydrography and Oceanography for Türkiye, and tables of local administrations are among the main sources.

Tide tables are organized in two basic structures: (1) Standard ports: Full annual HW/LW time and heights are given in tabular form. (2) Secondary/subordinate ports: Time and altitude correction factors are given relative to a standard reference port; These factors are applied to the tables of the standard port and the calculation is made for the secondary port.
Gelgit tabloları standart limanlar için: Tide tables give HW/LW times and heights in UT for standard ports.
Gelgit tablolarında spring ve neap arası: In tide tables, the transition between spring and neap can be traced from the systematic increase or decrease in each day's HW/LW height values. In almanacs or annual tables, the correlation between moon phases and tidal amplitude is clearly visible.

If the LAT datum is used, the tide height is always positive or zero (because LAT is the lowest level). If the actual water level had fallen below the LAT, the tide height would have been negative; This is an unusual situation.

Gelgitin ana kaynağı, Ay’ın Dünya üzerin: The main source of tides is the differential gravitational force of the Moon on the Earth. The Moon pulls more strongly on the water mass on the side closer to the Earth; The water swells on this side. On the other hand, a bulge forms on the opposite side of the Earth due to the centrifugal effect (the force resulting from the rotation around the center of gravity of the Earth-Moon system). This is why there are two opposing tidal swells on Earth at the same time.

Gemiler dengelerini korumak için boş sey: In order to maintain their balance, ships take in ballast water when cruising empty and pump this water when they take on cargo. However, with the received water, microscopic organisms, larvae and pathogens are carried from one ecosystem to another. These species, which have no natural enemies in the target area, can multiply rapidly and destroy native life and damage fisheries and infrastructure. The BWM Convention was established to manage this invisible but serious environmental threat. The essence of the solution is to either replace the ballast water before discharge or treat it to kill/remove any living creatures in it.

The second is to continue using cheap high-sulfur fuel and clean the exhaust with a scrubber (EGCS); There are open circuit, closed circuit and hybrid types, but washwater discharge is subject to pH, PAH and turbidity criteria and some ports prohibit open circuit discharge. The third is to switch to sulfur-free alternative fuels such as LNG or methanol. Cost, investment and operational results of each route are different.

The main tool is the inventory of hazardous materials on board (Inventory of Hazardous Materials, IHM); This inventory is kept up to date throughout the life cycle of the ship and given to the facility before dismantling.

Genel avarya (GA) ilkesi neyi düzenler?: What does the general average (GA) principle regulate?
Genel avarya (General Average, GA), orta: General average (GA) is the principle that when a deliberate and reasonable sacrifice is made to save the ship and cargo from a common maritime danger (e.g. giving water to the cargo to extinguish the fire, throwing the cargo overboard to float the ship) or when an extraordinary expense occurs, this loss is shared among all saved values (ship + cargo + freight) in proportion to the value. In other words, the damage suffered by one party for the common good is borne by everyone proportionally. GA is calculated for the parties by an average commissioner/dispatcher in accordance with the York-Antwerp Rules.

Genişleyen kare (expanding square) arama: The expanding square search pattern is one of the most frequently used patterns of IAMSAR and is particularly chosen when there is a single, relatively reliable datum point (last known position or calculated drift position) and a single search instrument is in the field. The logic is simple: the search tool starts from the datum, follows a square spiral that grows from the center outward in perpendicular turns; Each leg extends from the previous one by a certain fixed increment (a distance determined by the scanning range, i.e. the effective viewing/detection width of the vehicle). While this pattern scans the most likely region around the datum first and most intensively, the search expands from the inside out rather than the outside in, gradually reaching surrounding areas where uncertainty increases. The reason why it is preferred is that it offers both simplicity of application (single vehicle, navigation with simple turn commands) and the most efficient coverage rate in scenarios where datum reliability is high and drift uncertainty is low. If datum uncertainty is high or there is more than one asset, patterns that cover a larger area or are suitable for multi-vehicle coordination, such as parallel track or sector search, are preferred instead; This choice is the OSC's first tactical decision based on the conditions on the ground.

However, their functions are separated: EEXI is a compliance threshold under MARPOL Annex VI, if the ship does not pass this threshold it may become technically unnavigable and this is a statutory obligation. EVDI, on the other hand, is not a compliance threshold, but a ranking commercial rating (from A to G) and does not have any legal sanction. The practical significance of this is timing: when making a decision to charter a vessel, a charterer can pre-qualify by looking at RightShip's currently published GHG Rating, without waiting to see if EEXI has been formally inspected. So EVDI is a trade early warning system that comes into play before the formal verification process of EEXI; If a ship technically meets EEXI but has a low GHG Rating, it may still be an undesirable option for some environmentally conscious charterers.

GMDSS dört deniz alanı tanımlar ve her a: GMDSS defines four sea areas, and each area is determined by the infrastructure technology that provides coverage. Area A1 is the area under DSC (Digital Selective Calling) coverage of at least one VHF shore station; its typical range is 20–30 nautical miles. Area A2 is the area outside A1 but under DSC coverage of an MF (Medium Frequency) coast station; its range typically extends to around 100–150 nautical miles. Area A3 is the area outside A1 and A2 but under Inmarsat satellite coverage; This coverage includes approximately 70°N – 70°S latitudes. Area A4 covers areas other than A1, A2 and A3; mainly in the polar regions, where HF (High Frequency) radio communication is the main means of communication.

Göz (eye), olgunlaşmış bir tropikal sikl: The eye is the approximately circular calm region located at the center of rotation of a mature tropical cyclone. Its typical diameter is between 20–60 km; However, 'pinhole' eyes that can narrow down to 8–10 km in very intense, compact systems and eyes that exceed 100 km in weak or very wide systems have also been observed. As a general rule, a small and sharply circumscribed eye indicates a concentrated and violent system. Within the eye, surface wind often drops below 10–15 knots, precipitation ceases, and the sky may partially or completely clear; The stars can be seen at night and the sun can be seen during the day. The lowest pressure of the system at sea level is measured at the center of the eye; In severe hurricanes, this value drops below 950 hPa and in record systems, it drops below 900 hPa. The eye is also the 'warm core' of the system: due to the compressive heating of the collapsing air, the inside of the eye is at intermediate levels 5–10°C warmer than the surrounding atmosphere at the same altitude. This warm core is the key thermodynamic feature that distinguishes tropical cyclones from mid-latitude low pressures (cold core systems). When looked up from inside the eye, the eyewall clouds appear like a giant stadium tribune rising all around, which is called the 'stadium effect'.

Gözün açık ve sıcak olmasının temel nede: What is the main reason why the eye is open and warm?
Gözün en sinsi tehlikesi, atmosferdeki s: The most insidious danger to the eye is that the calmness in the atmosphere is not reflected in the sea. Even if the wind calms down, the sea inside the eye is in a completely chaotic 'confused/pyramidal sea' state, formed by the convergence of waves produced from all directions of the system to the center. Sequences of waves coming from different directions overlap, producing pyramidal, steep and unpredictable waves; It is impossible to predict the wave direction because there is no wind to regulate the waves. These conditions make the ship's rolling and pitching movements unsynchronized and unpredictable; A favorable environment is created for dangerous dynamic stability events, including parametric roll. Many ships throughout history have been injured in the eye or were caught unprepared for the second half of the storm, thinking that the wind had stopped and the storm was over. The critical fact is this: during eye passage, the wind returns from the OPPOSITE direction before entering. If the diameter of the eye is 30 km and the forward speed of the system is 15 knots, the calm period may last only 30–60 minutes; then the opposite side eyewall comes in full intensity with no gradual increase. The barometer reads its lowest value during this transition; The lowest reading means 'the center is above us', not 'danger is over'.
Gözün Tanımı ve Fiziksel Özellikleri: Definition and Physical Characteristics of the Eye
Gözün varlığı iki temel fiziksel mekaniz: The existence of the eye is the result of two basic physical mechanisms. The first is dynamic balance: the air flowing spirally towards the center of the cyclone gradually accelerates as it approaches the center due to the conservation of angular momentum (like an ice skater accelerating when he gathers his arms). At a certain radius, the centrifugal force balances the pressure gradient force pulling the air in, and the air cannot be brought any further into the center; This balance radius determines the inner boundary of the eyewall and therefore the size of the eye. All the moist air flowing in is forced to rise violently above this ring—this is how the eyewall's giant cumulonimbus tower is fed. The second mechanism is related to subsidence: some of the air that rises within the eyewall and discharges outwards at the top returns to the eye and collapses downwards there. The collapsing air is compressed and heated adiabatically; The relative humidity of the heated air decreases, clouds dissolve and the sky clears. This is why the eye is both open and warm. The eye becomes apparent on satellite and radar images as the system exceeds tropical storm strength and begins to mature (usually as sustained winds approach 64 knots); The emergence of a clear and symmetrical eye is one of the most reliable signs that the system is strengthened.

GPS (Global Positioning System), Amerika:
GPS (Global Positioning System) is a space-based satellite navigation system developed by the American Department of Defense and opened to full capacity for civilian use since 1995. The system consists of at least 24 active satellites positioned in various orbits around the Earth, and these satellites constantly emit strong time signals. A receiver on Earth calculates its own position by receiving these signals.

The revolutionary importance of GPS in terms of maritime is that it offers continuous, automatic and high-accuracy position determination. GPS works day and night, in all weather conditions, in every ocean; The sextant has become a complement to radar and visual positioning and has become the primary data source of modern ECDIS systems.

However, GPS also carries the danger of blind trust. Interrupting, jamming or spoofing the signal coming from satellites can disable GNSS systems or cause incorrect location indication. Therefore, STCW and IMO define GPS as a supporting tool; navigators must maintain radar, astronomy and conventional positioning proficiency.

The term 'pseudo' indicates that the error in the receiver clock adds error to the distance.
GPS alıcısında oluşan toplam konum hatas: The total position error occurring at the GPS receiver is a combination of different error components. Satellite clock and orbit errors, atmospheric delays (ionosphere/troposphere), receiver clock error, multipath reflection and receiver noise magnify the total error. At moments when the satellite geometry is weak (high DOP), the same error size produces larger deviations in position.

(3) Multipath: If the signal hits buildings or other structures and reaches the receiver through different paths, an error occurs; It becomes evident at port entrances and near cities. The intersection of 3 spheres obtained with 3 satellites theoretically gives two points; The point outside the earth is automatically eliminated and the 3D position is obtained.

After loading, the grain settles a bit, leaving space at the top; When the ship lurches, the grain sliding into this gap moves the center of gravity to one side and causes the ship to take a permanent inclination to that side. This tendency disrupts balance and can lead to the risk of capsizing in overlapping rolls. The code aims to calculate this shear moment and ensure that the ship still has sufficient stability.

Grain Code'un teknik özü, tahıl kaymasın: The technical essence of the Grain Code is to calculate the heeling moment resulting from grain shifting and prove that the ship's stability reserve is sufficient for this. The calculation uses a volumetric method based on bin geometry: in fully filled bins, it is assumed that the grain will shift towards the upper space at a certain angle (by default, approximately 15°) after settling, while in partially filled bins, a larger shift (approximately 25°) is possible. These assumed shifts produce an overturning moment for each hold, and the total moment is compared to the ship's stability curve. Partially full warehouses are therefore the riskiest; Filling as fully as possible and smooth trimming is preferred. The ship's approved grain loading booklet contains these calculations for different loading situations and the captain makes the loading plan accordingly.

Grup A yüklerde, nem belirli bir eşiği a: In Group A loads, if the humidity exceeds a certain threshold, the load changes from solid to fluid behavior (liquefaction) due to the vibration and movement of the ship. The fluidized load may slide to one side, causing a sudden and dangerous collapse, or even capsizing. To prevent this, the moisture content of the load must be below the Transportable Moisture Limit (TML) value. TML is usually determined as 90% of the Flow Moisture Point. If in doubt the captain may carry out a simple field check such as a 'can test', but the official decision is based on the laboratory certificate. If the humidity exceeds the TML, the load is rejected.
Grup A yükleri için kodun en önemli sayı: The code's most important numerical concept for Group A loads is the Transportable Moisture Limit (TML): the maximum moisture content at which the load can be safely transported, typically set at 90% of the flow moisture point (FMP). The actual moisture content of the load must be below this limit. Laboratory tests (Proctor/Fagerberg, flow table) and a rapid 'can/should test' in the field are used to confirm this. The loader must provide the ship with a cargo declaration containing TML and actual humidity values; Group A cargo should not be accepted without this document or without a moisture test.
Grup A yüklerinin güvenli taşınması, nem: Safe transportation of Group A loads relies on humidity control. The actual humidity of the cargo must be below the Transportable Humidity Limit (TML); TML is generally determined as 90% of the Flow Moisture Point (FMP). FMP is the moisture threshold at which the load changes from solid to fluid behavior. Accredited laboratory tests are used to determine these values: Methods such as Proctor/Fagerberg test, flow table test and penetration test are suitable for different load types. A 'can test' (putting the sample in a container and tamping it) can be done in the field as a quick preliminary check, but it is not a substitute for laboratory testing. The loader must provide the ship with a signed cargo information form (cargo declaration) containing TML and actual humidity values, and this document and the tests must date at most a certain number of days ago; otherwise the load is rejected.

GT'nin salt bir ölçüm değil, bir düzenle: The fact that GT functions as a regulatory key rather than a mere measurement creates a disproportionately large difference in liability between ships just above and below the threshold. For example, the 500 GT threshold introduces many of SOLAS' certification requirements for cargo ships (such as Safety Construction, Safety Equipment) and the ISM Code's mandatory SMC/DOC regime; While a ship of 499 GT remains exempt from this heavy certification and management system burden, a ship reaching 500 GT faces many new statutory obligations at the same time. A similar break is seen in the MLC Certificate requirement. This sharp threshold effect can become a conscious engineering goal for ship designers and shipowners: in this approach, known as 'tonnage optimisation', the internal volume of a ship is designed to be kept below the threshold without significantly sacrificing capacity – for example, by leaving certain above-deck areas partially open or creating voids that are not included in the volume calculation. This practice is sometimes criticized by regulatory authorities because it can create a mismatch between the ship's actual carrying capacity and the safety and labor standards regime to which it is subject; The IMO and some flag states have reviewed their tonnage calculation rules from time to time in order to limit such 'threshold gaming'.

Güvenlik seviyeleri arasındaki geçiş, kâ: The transition between security levels is not just a classification on paper; Triggers visible tangible changes on the ship. Level 1 (normal) covers permanent minimum measures: control of access points, random patrol on deck, entry to the ship with ID check. When moving to Level 2 (escalated), access control is tightened, typically in response to regional threat intelligence or a specific incident: additional personnel are assigned to the gangway, visitor and cargo checks are conducted more frequently and in greater detail, entries into restricted areas are recorded, the frequency of night patrols is increased, and security information sharing with neighboring ships/port facility is intensified. Transition to Level 3 (extraordinary) refers to urgent measures taken against a concrete and imminent threat: cargo operations may be stopped, access to the ship may be completely restricted or limited to authorized security personnel only, coordinated evacuation with the port facility or port departure scenarios may be activated. At each level transition, a Declaration of Security (DoS) is expected to be signed between the SSO, CSO and PFSO and the implemented measures are recorded.

The intern does not have the authority to independently approve plans; Everything he prepares is checked by the Second Officer and the Captain. The trainee never participates in these tasks as an independent responsible person, but under the direct supervision of a deck officer or experienced crew member. The aim at this stage is to identify the main route corridor and avoid major obstacles. Large-scale maps are used during the coastal approach, strait passage, narrow water navigation and harbor maneuver phases. These maps make it possible to manage shoals, restricted areas, sectoral lights and buoy arrays that are directly related to the draft of the ship.

Harita ölçeği, harita üzerindeki bir uzu: Map scale is expressed as the ratio of a length on the map to the actual length on earth and is written as 1:50 000, 1:25 000, 1:10 000. In this expression, as the denominator decreases, the scale increases and the detail increases; As the denominator increases, the scale decreases and the detail decreases. In maritime, a large-scale map is a map with a numerically small denominator. Harbor maps are therefore large scale; Offshore maps are small scale.
Harita ölçeği, mesafe ölçümünün doğruluğ: Map scale also directly affects the accuracy of distance measurement. As the scale decreases, a measurement error of millimeters on the map can correspond to hundreds of meters in reality. For this reason, distance measurement, location marking and route correction should be done on the largest scale map possible. The same principle applies to route measurement; An error of a few degrees, which seems insignificant on a small scale, can carry the ship out of the channel on a large scale.

Harmonize sörvey ve sertifika sistemi (H: The harmonized survey and certification system (HSSC) ensures the harmonization of all mandatory survey dates. Thanks to this system, operational interruption is minimized by combining surveys for different certificates of the ship as much as possible.
Harmonized Survey System (HSS), farklı s: Harmonized Survey System (HSS) combines surveys required by different conventions (SOLAS, MARPOL, Load Line) in a common schedule; This is to prevent a ship from being constantly interrupted by independent surveys at different times of the year. Annual surveys may be conducted within a ±3 month window around the anniversary of the certificate; This flexibility ensures that the ship can meet the surveyor regardless of which port or operation it is in at that time. The interim survey is scheduled for the second to third year, the renewal survey for the end of the fifth year, and the renewal window carries a similar tolerance (usually 3 months before – 3 months after). This window system is not pure bureaucracy for the shipowner, but a concrete operational planning tool: charter contracts, dry dock appointments and crew changes are arranged according to these windows, since a survey outside the window effectively invalidates the certificate and subjects the ship to docking or PSC detention. That's why operations departments treat the survey schedule as an integral input into route planning.

Each type has a different characteristic temperature and humidity profile: mT mass is hot and humid and poses a risk of fog, while cP mass is cold and dry and can produce sudden cooling and strong winds.

Height of Tide refers to how many meters above the chart datum the water level is at a certain time and port. Only HW and LW times and heights can be read directly from the tide table; The water height must be calculated for every moment in between.

This calculation can be done by three basic methods: (1) Rule of Twelfths: simple and fast, but approximate; (2) Sine curve interpolation: a more accurate mathematical method; (3) Admiralty tide curve (tidal curve): the most accurate method, used especially in ports with complex or irregular tidal profiles. The rule of 12 and the tidal curve method are generally required in maritime exams.
