Her gemi için tek bir AB üye devleti 'ad: A single EU member state is appointed as the 'administrating authority' for each ship and operationally this state is the addressee of all MRV and EUA obligations of the ship. For EU-flagged ships, this is directly the flag state; For non-EU flagged ships, the determination is made according to the member state that the ship visited the most EU ports in the previous four monitoring periods and is announced in the list published by the Commission. If a ship has never called at an EU port or if the data is insufficient, the first member state it called is considered the authority for that period. In practice, this means that the administrative point of contact from which the shipowner will have the MRV monitoring plan approved, select the verifying body and receive the Document of Compliance may vary, so the fleet manager must follow which authority applies to each ship and that authority's national implementing practices (language, portal, time tolerances). In case of a change of authority, obligations towards the old and new authority may overlap during the transition period.

Her gemi yıllık performansına göre A'dan: Each ship receives a rating from A to E based on its annual performance: A represents best, E represents worst performance; C is the acceptable middle level. The critical feature of this rating is that the baselines tighten each year: yesterday's C performance may drop to D a few years later due to the required mitigation, meaning the ship is left behind by simply remaining the same. A ship that receives D for three consecutive years or E for any year must prepare a mandatory corrective action plan. This mechanism pushes the fleet towards continuous improvement.

Her geminin yapısal özelliklerinden kayn: Every ship has radar blind sectors caused by structural features (chimneys, cranes, container stacks, etc.). These sectors should be marked on the bridge and known to the officer of the watch. Target detection is not possible in blind sectors; In this case, other radar (if available), AIS and spotter information are used. Sea clutter can mask small targets; Especially wooden boats, rafts and small fishing vessels are difficult to detect on the radar screen. Knowing these limitations, radar should not be accepted as the only reliable source, multiple source verification should be done.
Her gemiyi her seferinde denetlemek imkâ: Since it is impossible to inspect every ship every time, PSC directs its resources according to risk. A risk profile is calculated based on the ship's age, type, flag and class performance, and past inspection results; The ship is classified as High (HRS), Standard (SRS) or Low (LRS) risk and inspection frequency is determined accordingly. The inspection deepens from the initial inspection, which examines the certificate and general condition, to a more detailed inspection in case of 'clear grounds' (suspicious findings) and a mandatory extended inspection on tankers/passenger ships. Operational checks such as fire and lifesaving drills and rudder tests can also be performed.

IAPP is the bridge from classical pollution control to climate regulation. SEEMP (Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan), which is mandatory to be kept on board, has three parts: general efficiency management (Part I), IMO DCS data collection plan (Part II) and CII management plan (Part III). Thus, under the IAPP certificate, both the ship's design efficiency (EEXI) and operational carbon performance (CII) are monitored. The scope of the certificate has expanded over time: fuel or scrubber verification for sulfur (SOx) compliance, registration of ozone depleting substances (ODS – halon, CFC), VOC management plan for crude oil tankers and approved ship incinerators are also evaluated under this certificate. Missing NOx file, SOx incompatibility, or SEEMP deficiency leads to PSC deficiency and possible retention; Without the certificate, the ship cannot make international voyages.
IAPP'nin en teknik unsuru, gemideki 130: The most technical element of the IAPP is the NOx Technical File for each diesel engine above 130 kW on board. This file documents that the engine's nitrogen oxide emissions comply with the Tier I, II or III limits applied depending on the year of manufacture and cruising region, and identifies all 'adjustable components' (injector, fuel pump timing, turbocharger, valve adjustment) that affect the engine's emissions. The important thing is that the maintenance of the engine is kept within the approved parameters in this file: if the emission characteristic of the engine is changed during a maintenance or parts replacement, this must be re-verified by an approved method (e.g. onboard monitoring or parameter control). Tier III applies only in NOx Emission Control Areas (NECA) and usually requires additional technology such as selective catalytic reduction (SCR) or exhaust gas recirculation (EGR). If the file is not up-to-date, it will cause a deficiency in the PSC.
IAPP'nin teknik kalbi iki ana kirleticid: The technical heart of IAPP is two main pollutants. On the NOx side, every diesel engine above 130 kW has a NOx Technical Dossier and is subject to Tier I, II or (in NECA regions) Tier III limits depending on the year of engine manufacture; Engine maintenance (injector, turbocharger, timing) directly affects this harmony. On the SOx side, compliance is achieved with either low sulfur fuel or an approved scrubber and is documented with BDNs and fuel samples. Over time, the scope of this certification has expanded: ODS registrations, VOC management plan for crude oil tankers, approved ship burners and from 2023 EEXI verification have also been added to the IAPP.

IBC Code, dökme tehlikeli kimyasal taşıy: IBC Code is based on the principle of designing ships carrying bulk hazardous chemicals according to the risk posed by the cargo. The logic is this: the more dangerous the substance transported (toxicity, flammability, environmental damage), the higher the survivability of the ship should be. Therefore, ships are classified as Types 1, 2 and 3; Type 1 carries the most hazardous loads and is subject to the most stringent subdivision, damage stability and tank layout requirements (tanks furthest outside the hull, limited in volume). Thus, the damage that the most dangerous cargo may cause to the environment and the ship in the event of a collision or grounding is minimized.
IBC Code'un tasarım mantığı, geminin hay: The design logic of the IBC Code is to determine the survivability of the ship according to the danger of the cargo it carries. Type 1 ships carry the most dangerous cargoes and are subject to the most stringent requirements: their tanks are located furthest from the hull, their volume is limited, and damage stability criteria are the strictest; The aim is to minimize the likelihood of spilling the most dangerous cargo in a collision or grounding. Type 2 and Type 3 ships have gradually relaxed requirements for less hazardous cargo. Each cargo is identified with the minimum ship type it requires in the list in Chapter 17; A ship can only carry products authorized in its certificate (Certificate of Fitness) and only if the ship type conditions they require are met. Partitioning, double skin and damage stability calculations form the basis of this classification.
IBC Code'un Tip 1/2/3 ayrımı soyut bir e: The IBC Code's Type 1/2/3 distinction is not an abstract labeling, but an engineering rule with direct geometric and volumetric consequences. The type of ship required for the transportation of a substance is determined in the list in Chapter 17 according to the seriousness of the damage that that substance may cause to the environment and human health in an accident; toxicity, flammability, corrosivity and reactivity are the inputs to this assessment. For the most dangerous cargoes that must be carried in Type 1, the minimum distance of the cargo tank to the ship's shell and collision bulkhead is kept as wide as possible; This reduces the possibility of the tank being punctured in the event of a side collision or grounding impact to the bow area. By the same logic, the maximum volume that a single tank can carry in Type 1 ships is strictly limited (approximately 1250 m³), because the amount that can be spilled in case of damage is kept under control with this upper limit. In Type 2 ships, distance and volume requirements are gradually relaxed, while in Type 3 they are relatively least restrictive. This triple system allows cargo of different hazard levels to be carried together within the same ship hull, but each with physical protection appropriate to its own risk level.

IGC Code, kargo tanklarını taşıdıkları b: The IGC Code classifies cargo tanks according to the pressure/temperature regime they carry and leak management philosophy. Self-contained tanks are of three subtypes: Type C is designed as a pressure vessel and generally does not require a secondary barrier (common on LPG and ethylene vessels); Types A and B are suitable for lower pressure, larger volume, cryogenic loads and require a secondary barrier (Type B partial, Type A full secondary barrier). Membrane tanks (GTT Mark III, NO96) are a thin system of barrier and insulation layers supported by the ship's hull and are standard on large LNG carriers. Material selection is critical in cryogenic conditions: ordinary steel becomes brittle in extreme cold, so special low-temperature steels, nickel alloys or stainless steel are used on surfaces in contact with the cargo. The tank type also determines the ship's overall damage stability and layout design.
IGC Code, LNG, LPG, etilen ve amonyak gi: The IGC Code governs the unique hazards of tankers carrying liquefied gases such as LNG, LPG, ethylene and ammonia. These cargoes are kept in liquid form either at very low temperature (cryogenic, approximately -163°C for LNG) or under high pressure; When they leak, they can expand rapidly and form flammable or toxic clouds, and their extreme cold can make the steel body brittle. The Code designs these ships to the highest technical standards, making gas tankers the most sophisticated and tightly regulated ships at sea. The main purpose is to keep the cargo under control under all circumstances and isolated from areas where people are present.
IGC tank tipleri: A (tam ikincil bariyer: IGC tank types: A (full secondary barrier), B (partial), C (pressurized, no barrier), membrane (LNG)
IGC'nin teknik kalbi kargo tankı tasarım: The technical heart of the IGC is the cargo tank design. Tanks can be freestanding (type A, B, C), membrane or integral; Each type is based on a different pressure/temperature and leak management philosophy. The critical concept is the secondary barrier: if the primary tank leaks, there is a second layer of protection to prevent cold liquid from reaching the ship's hull and brittle it. The interbarrier space is constantly monitored for temperature and gas, so that the slightest leak is detected early. The design of membrane tanks (GTT Mark III, NO96) is the most advanced example of this double protection principle.
IGC'nin temel emniyet ilkesi, soğuk karg: IGC's basic safety principle is that refrigerated cargo should not reach the ship's hull under any circumstances; because a cryogenic leak can instantly embrittle the steel and lead to structural collapse. Therefore, a secondary barrier is envisaged that is activated in case the primary tank leaks, and this barrier must be able to safely hold the leaking liquid for a certain period of time. The interbarrier space between the primary and secondary barrier and the surrounding spaces are constantly monitored for temperature and gas; A sudden temperature drop or gas detection gives early warning of even the slightest leak. This monitoring network is an integral part of the cargo control system and allows the crew to respond to a problem before it becomes a disaster.
IGF Code – 2017: Doğal gaz veya düşük pa: IGF Code – 2017: Safety requirements for ships using natural gas or low flash point fuel.
IGF Code kapsamında gaz yakıtlı gemi eği: Adding gas fueled ship training within the scope of IGF Code
IGF Code yakıt gaz sisteminin tasarım ve: The IGF Code regulates the design and operation of the fuel gas system.
IGF Code, gaz yakıtın gemide depolanması: The IGF Code binds the storage and distribution of gaseous fuel on board to detailed technical requirements. LNG is generally kept at cryogenic temperature in insulated Type C pressure tanks; The tank layout is positioned at a certain distance from the hull so that it will not be damaged in collision and grounding. The fuel preparation room and fuel valve units (TVU/GVU) in the engine room control the pressure and temperature of the gas. The bunkering station ensures fuel intake from a safe point, with leak collection and emergency separation mechanisms. All these systems are designed on the 'double barrier' principle: at each point where the gas is captured, there are two independent layers of protection (e.g. double-walled pipe and ventilated enclosure) to ensure that even in the event of a single fault, the gas does not reach occupied areas.
IGF Code, geleneksel SOLAS bölümlerinin: The IGF Code deliberately departs from the 'prescriptive' approach seen in most traditional SOLAS chapters, as gaseous fuel technologies can be implemented in different arrangements on each ship and prescribing a single standard design restricts innovation. Instead, 'alternative designs and regulations' are opened for fuels or regulations that are outside Part A-1 and do not yet have a detailed prescription: the designer must prove through risk analysis that the solution he proposes is at least as safe as the prescribed standard. The process typically begins with a HAZID (Hazard Identification) study; Here, possible hazard scenarios at each stage of design (storage, pipeline, bunkering, emergency) are systematically listed. Then, HAZOP (Hazard and Operability Study) is performed for critical scenarios; In this study, each system element is questioned with 'deviation words' (more, less, none, reverse) and failure chains and their consequences are detailed. The output of these analyzes is evaluated by an independent third party (usually a classification society) and presented to management; Approval is a formal decision that the documented risk level of the design is acceptable. This process ensures that the design for each new fuel, from LNG to ammonia, is shaped by real-world failure probabilities.
IGF Code, gemilerin geleneksel fuel oil: The IGF Code was established to manage new risks arising as ships switch from conventional fuel oil to LNG and other low flash point fuels. These fuels have an environmental advantage but are a safety challenge: when leaked as a gas, it spreads rapidly, is stored at very low temperatures, and forms an explosive mixture in a narrow range. The distinctive approach of the code is that it is goal-based rather than writing every detail in advance: the designer must prove the security of the system through structured risk analysis such as HAZID/HAZOP and obtain administration/class approval. This flexibility allows nascent fuel technologies to develop safely.
IGF Code'un ayırt edici yönü, her ayrınt: The distinguishing aspect of the IGF Code is that it is goal-based and risk-based, rather than prescribing every detail. The designer must prove the security of the system through structured risk analyzes such as HAZID and HAZOP and obtain administration/class approval; This flexibility allows nascent fuel technologies to develop safely. Although the code currently covers LNG predominantly, new fuels are coming into focus with decarbonisation: interim guidelines are in place for methanol, requirements are being developed for ammonia (which presents additional challenges due to its toxicity) and hydrogen. Each new fuel brings unique hazards (flash point, toxicity, flame speed, storage temperature) and the IGF's risk-based framework is the way to manage this diversity. Crews are required to receive special gas fuel training under STCW.
IGF'nin temel mühendislik felsefesi 'çif: IGF's core engineering philosophy is 'double barrier': at each point where the fuel is held there are two independent layers of protection to ensure that even in the event of a single fault, the gas does not reach occupied areas. Fuel tanks, pipelines and connections are designed with this logic; Double-walled pipes and vented casings are used to catch and safely expel gas leaks. The engine room is divided into 'gas safe' and 'gas dangerous' zones; Electrical equipment is selected in accordance with this classification. Gas detection systems constantly monitor and when the threshold is exceeded, automatic emergency shutdown (ESD) is activated and immediately cuts off the fuel flow.

II-1, geminin su altı bütünlüğünü çok ka: II-1 secures the ship's underwater integrity in a multi-layered manner. The principle of subdivision divides the ship into compartments with watertight bulkheads; the aim is for the ship to remain afloat and stable when one or more compartments take on water. For passenger and cargo ships after 2009, the probabilistic damage stability method (required A index ≥ reached A index) is used, which evaluates damage scenarios together with their probabilities. Section; Covers type and closing times of watertight doors, double bottom requirements, damage control plans and bilge/ballast pumping arrangements. On the machinery and electrical side, it regulates the redundancy of main and auxiliary engines, emergency power sources (emergency generator), steering gear (main and auxiliary system, test requirements) and rudder control; The aim is to ensure that a single malfunction does not render the ship unmanageable.
II-2 yangın koruma/algılama/söndürmeyi;: II-2 fire protection/detection/suppression; II-1 regulates structure/machine, III regulates LSA, IV regulates GMDSS.
II-2, yangını üç stratejiyle ele alır: ö: II-2 addresses fire with three strategies: prevention, containment, and suppression. Prevention; This is achieved through the restriction of flammable materials, safe design of fuel/oil systems and control of ignition sources. Containment delays the spread of fire in one space to neighboring spaces by dividing the ship into main vertical zones with class A and B fire compartments (different endurance times from A-60 to A-0); Fire doors, dampers and emergency stop of ventilation complete this system. Perception; It instantly determines the location of the fire with smoke and heat detectors, manual alarm points and central panels on the bridge. Suppression varies by space: constant CO₂/foam/water mist for engine room, sprinklers for accommodation spaces, foam monitors for deck. The chapter also regulates the design of escape routes, emergency lighting, firefighter equipment (SCBA, EEBD) and additional measures specific to tankers (inert gas, foam).
III, kazadan sonra hayatta kalmayı hem d: III regulates survival after the accident, both in terms of equipment and organization. On the equipment side, survival craft (fully enclosed, free-falling lifeboats, life rafts), rescue boat, lowering devices (davit) and personal equipment (life jacket, immersion suit, TPA) are determined in terms of number and performance; Marine Evacuation System (MES) is prescribed for rapid evacuation on passenger ships. On the organizational side, it is mandatory for each ship to have a muster list (fire chart), each crew member must know their duty in the event of an emergency, and muster stations must be marked. Drills are the heart of this section: abandoned ship and fire drills are carried out at regular intervals, lifeboat launches are carried out and recorded at regular intervals; Familiarization training is given to newly joined personnel. The detail of technical standards is left to the LSA Code.

IMDG Code, deniz yoluyla taşınan binlerc: IMDG Code makes thousands of dangerous goods transported by sea manageable with a single international system. Each substance is assigned a UN number and a standard Proper Transport Name (PSN); Thus, whatever the trade name of a chemical, it is recognized in the same way and subject to the same rules in every port of the world. The basic logic of the code is to first classify the hazard, then apply the packaging, signs, documents and stacking rules appropriate to this class. IMDG Code'un sınıflandırması, her madden: The IMDG Code's classification is based around nine classes that indicate the predominant hazard of each substance, and many are further subdivided. Class 1 (explosives) has six compliance subsections; Class 2 gases (2.1 flammable, 2.2 non-flammable/non-toxic, 2.3 toxic); Class 3 flammable liquids; Class 4 flammable solids, spontaneously combusting substances and those that emit flammable gases when in contact with water (4.1/4.2/4.3); Class 5 oxidizers and organic peroxides (5.1/5.2); Class 6 toxic and infectious substances (6.1/6.2); Class 7 radioactive substances; Class 8 corrosive substances; Class 9 is reserved for other hazardous materials (including lithium batteries, marine pollutants). Packaging groups (I high, II medium, III low hazard) determine the degree of danger and the required packaging strength. These two dimensions together define how an item will be packaged and handled.

IMDG'nin en hayati operasyonel bölümü ay: The most vital operational part of the IMDG is segregation rules: substances that can react dangerously with each other (e.g. acids and cyanides, oxidizers and flammables) must be transported over certain distances or in separate compartments. The segregation table and special provisions determine which items should be kept side by side and which should be kept separately. The stacking plan is made according to these rules; below/above deck, distance from heat sources and ventilation are also taken into account. An incorrect separation may cause two individually harmless loads to combine and produce fire or toxic gas.
IMDG'nin en hayati operasyonel bölümü, b: The most vital operational part of IMDG is segregation rules, which prevent substances that may react dangerously with each other from being transported together. The segregation table determines which classes will be 'kept out', 'segregated', 'separated one bay/hatch apart' or 'separated one bay apart'; For example, acids and cyanides, oxidizers and flammables must be kept at certain distances, otherwise two harmless charges may combine and produce fire or poisonous gas. Stowage rules regulate whether each item should be carried above or below deck, how far away from heat sources and living quarters it should be carried, and what ventilation conditions are required. Safe packaging of containers and vehicles is coordinated with CTU Code, and lashing during transportation is coordinated with CSS Code.

The open circuit scrubber washes the sulfur compounds in the exhaust gas directly with sea water and discharges the acidified, heavy metal and PAH-containing water into the sea; While this may be considered acceptable in the open ocean when the dilution capacity is high, it raises local pollution concentration concerns in closed harbor basins, bottlenecks, or waters with sensitive ecosystems. For this reason, some countries and ports have partially or completely banned open circuit discharge (in their territorial waters or within port borders). As a result, a ship with an open-circuit scrubber must check in advance in its voyage planning which ports or regions allow open-circuit discharge, switch to closed-loop mode in prohibited areas (in hybrid systems) or switch to compatible low-sulfur fuel in that region; This limits the expected operational flexibility of the scrubber investment to regional constraints.

IMSBC Code'un pratik omurgası, 350'den f: The practical backbone of the IMSBC Code is load profiles (schedules) prepared separately for more than 350 bulk cargoes. Each profile; It includes the load description, group, stacking factor, hazards during transportation, ventilation and gas measurement requirements, loading/unloading precautions and emergency procedures. If a new cargo that is not listed is to be transported, a temporary transport permit must be obtained from the competent authorities. Trimming (even distribution of the load within the hold) is essential for both stability and structural load distribution; It is especially critical for liquefiable loads and to prevent structural stress. The loading operation is coordinated with BLU Code, which standardizes the communication and loading plan between the ship and the terminal; Unbalanced or too rapid loading can impose harmful bending/torsional stress on the hull, so the loading order and rate are monitored by a loading computer.
IMSBC Code'un tüm sınıflandırması üç gru: The entire classification of the IMSBC Code is built around three groups, with each group representing a different philosophy of hazards. Group A are cargoes that can liquefaction when containing moisture; The main risk is sudden loss of balance. Group B is cargo carrying chemical hazards; They can start a fire, deplete oxygen and suffocate the hold, emit toxic or flammable gas, or react dangerously with water/air. Group C are relatively harmless loads that neither liquefy nor pose chemical hazards (but even these can present risks such as structural overloading and dust). Some loads show both A and B properties (A&B). Knowing which group a load is in determines all the precautions to be taken (whether ventilation is open or closed, whether gas measurement is required, whether humidity testing is required); That's why group confirmation before installation is the critical first step.
IMSBC Code'un varlık nedeni, dökme katı: The raison d'être of the IMSBC Code is the deadly risks behind the innocent appearance of bulk solid cargoes. The most critical danger is liquefaction: fine-grained cargoes containing moisture (nickel ore, bauxite, some concentrates) can suddenly begin to behave like a liquid with the vibration and movement of the ship. In this case, the cargo slides in the hold, disrupts the ship's heeling balance and may cause capsizing within minutes. The code divides cargo into three groups according to their hazard characteristics: Group A is liquefiable cargo, Group B is those that carry chemical hazards (fire, poisonous gas, oxygen consumption), and Group C is those that do not carry both risks.

In-Water Survey (IWS), belirli koşullard: Although In-Water Survey (IWS) makes it possible to delay the need for a dry dock in certain conditions, it does not offer a true inspection alternative for some components because accurate assessment of these components requires complete drainage of water and direct access. Rudder pintle wear requires micron-level tolerance measurements that cannot be measured with the tactile sensitivity of the diver or ROV; This measurement is only reliable when the wake is taken out of the water and measured mechanically. Sea chest screens require visual and physical inspection for fouling and corrosion accumulated on the interior surface, underwater turbidity and access angle severely limit this inspection. The bow thruster tunnel and the propeller-bearing system inside it, as well as sensitive electronic casings such as the sonar dome, should similarly be examined outside the water, with direct view, and if necessary, by dismantling them. That is why the classification rules always define IWS as a 'conditional' alternative: ships meeting certain age, history and condition criteria are permitted for a limited number of successive periods, but in the case of these components the scope of IWS is either reduced or a dry dock is required directly.

Indian Ocean MoU bölgesinde, MoU'nun ort: In the Indian Ocean MoU region, the common rules of the MoU are often layered with strong national regimes. Australia's AMSA and South Africa's SAMSA are known for their stringent practices and focus areas (e.g. structural integrity, MLC, environmental compliance); Ships entering the ports of these countries must meet these national expectations as well as regional standards. Therefore, the most rational approach for ships entering the region is to research both the CIC themes at the MoU level and the specific requirements of the destination country in advance. Monitoring regional audit trends, addressing past deficiencies, and keeping evidence of discovery closure readily available is key to ensuring consistent alignment across these various regimes.
Indian Ocean MoU kuruldu – Hint Okyanusu: Indian Ocean MoU established – PSC cooperation between Indian Ocean coastal states begins
Indian Ocean MoU, Hint Okyanusu ve çevre: The Indian Ocean MoU coordinates port state control of 18 member states in and around the Indian Ocean; Members spread over a wide geography, from Australia to India, from South Africa to Iran and the coast of East Africa. This region hosts the busiest trade routes between Suez and the Straits of Malacca and a critical portion of the world's oil/container traffic. The MoU shares inspection data through the IOMIS regional system and identifies priority ships through risk-based targeting.
Indian Ocean MoU'nun belirgin bir özelli: A salient feature of the Indian Ocean MoU is the differences in inspection capacity between member states; Therefore, the MoU emphasizes strengthening regional standardization through auditor training programs and technical assistance. Inspection rates may vary depending on the capacity of the member state. Ships entering the region must consider the MoU's common rules as well as strong national regimes: Australia's AMSA and South Africa's SAMSA are known for their own stringent enforcement. As CIC campaigns are coordinated with the Paris and Tokyo MoUs, ships should review current themes and submit gap closure evidence in a timely manner.
Indian Ocean MoU'nun en zorlu yönetişim: The most challenging governance challenge of the Indian Ocean MoU is the extraordinary diversity of its membership base: on the one hand, there are countries with developed flag/port state infrastructure and experienced staff of inspectors, such as Australia, and on the other hand, small coastal states with limited administrative and financial resources, such as Eritrea, Comoros, Sudan or the Maldives. This gap poses the risk of inequity in inspection quality: even though they are bound by the same MoU framework, the number of inspectors, training level and equipment of one member port may be very different from another, threatening the consistency of targeting and deficiency detection. To offset this risk, the MoU attaches structural importance to capacity-building programmes: auditor trainers from experienced member states are sent, common audit manuals and checklists are standardized, IMO technical cooperation funds are directed to auditor training of junior members and infrastructure investment. The aim is that the inspection reflects the same basic quality and consistency no matter which port of call; Otherwise, ship operators may consciously choose weaker regulated ports, weakening the credibility of the entire regime.
Indian Ocean MoU'yu ayıran en belirgin ö: The most distinctive feature that distinguishes the Indian Ocean MoU is the differences in surveillance capacity between member states: the region covers a wide spectrum, from countries with developed PSC infrastructure (Australia, South Africa, India) to countries with limited resources. Therefore, the MoU pays special attention to auditor training programmes, technical assistance and standardization work; The aim is to ensure consistent inspection quality across all member ports. Inspection data is shared through IOMIS (Indian Ocean MoU Information System) and risk-based targeting is based on this data. The region has high control volume and strategic importance as it hosts the busiest trade routes between Suez and the Strait of Malacca; joint CIC campaigns are coordinated with the Paris and Tokyo MoUs.

IOMIS veri paylaşımının pratikteki değer: The practical value of IOMIS data sharing is the ability to uninterruptedly track a ship's footprint within the region. For example, if a ship is inspected at a port in India and flagged as high risk due to a serious structural deficiency, this information immediately reaches other member states via IOMIS; When the same ship calls at an Oman or South African port on its next voyage, the inspector of that port will see the current risk status of the ship and the previous finding, prioritize the inspection accordingly and usually subject it to a more comprehensive inspection. This chain mechanism makes substandard ships visible across the region that a single port cannot catch with its limited capacity, and prevents ship operators from being able to disguise poor performance in one port in another. Because risk-based targeting relies on this shared data, the timeliness and data quality of IOMIS determines the effectiveness of the entire system; Therefore, the MoU considers member states' timely and accurate entry of audit results into the system as an integral part of capacity building efforts.

IOPP Certificate (International Oil Poll: The IOPP Certificate (International Oil Pollution Prevention Certificate) certifies that a ship complies with oil pollution prevention equipment and procedures covered by MARPOL Annex I. It is mandatory for ships of 400 GT and above and (with a lower threshold) for oil tankers. The certificate has an integral annex: Form A for non-tank vessels, Form B for tankers; These annexes list in detail the anti-pollution equipment on board. The IOPP is valid for five years and is kept alive by annual and interim surveys; The supplement is updated when the hardware changes.
IOPP Certificate düzenleme, survey aralı: IOPP Certificate issuance, survey intervals and validity conditions.
IOPP Certificate'ın ayrılmaz ve aslında: An integral and indeed the most informative part of the IOPP Certificate is its supplement: Form A for non-tank ships, Form B for tankers. This annex lists all the oil pollution prevention equipment on board: capacity and type of oil-water separator (OWS), 15 ppm monitoring and alarm device, slop tank layout, cargo oil residue monitoring device (ODME), separated ballast tanks (SBT) and crude oil washing (COW) systems. During the inspection, the actual equipment on the ship is expected to match this list exactly; The supplement must be updated whenever a piece of equipment is changed or removed, otherwise there will be a discrepancy between the certificate and the actual situation, which is a PSC finding. Supplement is thus the official inventory of the ship's environmental equipment and the road map for inspection.
IOPP rejiminde en ciddi ihlaller donanım: The most serious violations in the IOPP regime revolve around registry fraud and bypass, not hardware. The devices known as 'magic pipes', which pump the bilge directly into the sea by bypassing the oil-water separator, and their concealment in the Oil Record Book are among the most severely punished maritime crimes worldwide; It results in millions of dollars in fines and imprisonment, especially under the APPS in the United States. It is therefore vital that the ORB is kept accurate, complete and honest. Without IOPP, the ship cannot sail, while MARPOL Annex I non-compliance will result in detention at PSC.
IOPP rejiminin denetlenebilirliğinin kal: The heart of the auditability of the IOPP regime is the Oil Record Book (ORB): Part I records engine room operations (bilge sorting, sludge transfer/burning, bunkering), Part II records cargo/ballast operations on tankers. Each entry indicates the type, quantity, time and location of the operation and is signed by the officer in charge and the master; The ledger is kept on the ship for a certain period of time (usually three years). ORB is one of the first documents examined in the audit because it reveals where and how the discharges are made. The most egregious violations do not revolve around hardware failure but registration fraud and bypass: 'magic pipe' assemblies bypassing the oil-water separator and their concealment in the ORB resulting in millions of dollars in fines and imprisonment under APPS, particularly in the US; Whistleblower rewards encourage the discovery of these violations. Therefore, keeping the ORB honest and complete is the most critical aspect of IOPP compliance.

In the engine room, the oil-water separator (OWS) reduces the oil in the bilge water below the legal limit of 15 ppm, and the 15 ppm alarm automatically stops the discharge when this limit is exceeded. ODM, slop tanks and separated ballast tanks (SBT) monitor cargo discharge in tankers and prevent dirty water from being discharged into the sea. ISGOTT, zorunlu bir sözleşme değil, ama: ISGOTT is not a mandatory contract, but it is the 'gold standard' that is actually expected to be adhered to in the oil tanker and terminal world. Regulations such as SOLAS, MARPOL and IGS Code tell what to do; ISGOTT explains step by step how to do this safely in the field. The stakes on tankers are uniquely high: the cargo is flammable, toxic and environmentally harmful, much of the operation is the joint responsibility of ship and shore (or another ship), and a single mistake can be catastrophic. ISGOTT standardizes this shared responsibility; Co-publishing OCIMF, ICS and IAPH ensures that both ship and terminal sides speak the same language. That's why ISGOTT practices are sought as actual reference in vetting audits.
ISGOTT'un kalbi, gemi ile terminal arası: The heart of ISGOTT is the management of the critical interface between ship and terminal. Before starting a transfer, the parties hold a pre-transfer (pre-cargo) meeting: the initial and maximum flow rate (pumping rate), the low flow rate during topping-up, the communication method to be used (VHF channel and backup), the emergency stop (ESD) signal, the maximum allowable manifold pressure and the procedure to be applied if communication is interrupted are clarified. All safety conditions are confirmed by the Ship-Shore Safety Checklist (SSSCL), which is filled out and signed by the ship and terminal representative together. ISGOTT 6 has redesigned this list from a 'box-filling' formality to a process in which each item is actually verified and reconfirmed at regular intervals.

Purpose, scope and definitions of the ISM Code.
ISM Code'un amacı: denizde emniyeti sağl: The purpose of the ISM Code is to ensure safety at sea, prevent human injury and loss of life, and protect the environment.
ISM Code'un ilk maddeleri, sistemin zemi: The first articles of the ISM Code lay the groundwork for the system. Article 1 clearly defines the purpose of the code: to ensure safety at sea, to prevent loss of life and injury and to avoid damage to the environment (especially the marine environment); For this reason, it requires every company to set safety targets. Clause 2 requires the company to establish a written safety and environmental protection policy and implement it at all levels of the organization. Article 3 defines the concept of 'company' and highlights a critical fact: ISM covers not only the ship but also the shore organization that operates it. If the owner and operator of the ship are different, the party actually managing the ship assumes ISM obligations and notifies the flag state. Thus, safety responsibility is not left unclear, but is attached to a concrete legal entity.
ISM dış denetiminin en temel mesleki tek: The most basic professional technique of ISM external auditing is to constantly test that the existence of a procedure is not the same as its implementation. The auditor is not satisfied with reading an SMS manual and seeing 'fire drills are held once a month'; It requires concrete evidence to verify this claim: signed exercise reports, photographs taken during the exercise, whether the crew remembers which task they undertook in that exercise, whether the dates of the test records of critical equipment (fire pump, emergency generator) match with the maintenance book. A 'major non-conformity' is not a single forgotten signature; It is a repeated or systemic failure that indicates a break in the system as a whole—situations exceed this threshold, for example, when no internal audit has been performed for months, a critical procedure is unknown to the entire crew, or a DPA is found to be not actually performing its duty. Such a finding could trigger suspension of the SMC (and therefore the DOC) because the auditor's conclusion is no longer 'there is a minor deficiency' but rather 'this system cannot be relied upon to actually work'.

It was rapidly developed following the September 11, 2001 attacks out of concern that commercial ships and ports could be a tool or target of terrorism. It operates based on SOLAS Chapter XI-2 and adopts a risk-based approach: first, threats and vulnerabilities are assessed (SSA), then concrete measures against them are linked to a plan (SSP). The code treats the ship not as an isolated unit but as a security system together with port facilities.

ISPS uyumu bir değerlendirmeyle başlar:: ISPS compliance begins with an assessment: Ship Security Assessment (SSA) systematically analyzes the threats to which the ship may be exposed and its vulnerabilities to them. This work is carried out under the responsibility of the CSO (Company Security Officer); It identifies critical equipment and areas (bridge, engine room, cargo control, access points), evaluates possible threat scenarios (unauthorized entry, stowaway, sabotage, weapons/explosive smuggling, use of the ship as a weapon) and reveals gaps in existing measures. SSA forms the basis of the ship's security plan; A poorly made evaluation leaves the entire plan based on it unfounded. Therefore, SSA is a disciplined process that combines a concrete site inspection and risk analysis.
ISPS, güvenliği atanmış sorumluluklar ve: ISPS embodies security through assigned responsibilities and daily practices. Onboard SSO is responsible for plan implementation, shoreside CSO is responsible for company level coordination, portside PFSO is responsible for facility security; This trio ensures uninterrupted security at the ship-port interface. In day-to-day operation, access control is central: the identity of everyone boarding is verified, visitors and contractors are registered, the gangway is constantly monitored. Restricted areas (bridge, engine room, radio room, cargo control) are closed to unauthorized access and marked. Security equipment – hidden alarm system (SSAS), AIS, CCTV, lighting and access control equipment – is tested regularly. SSAS is particularly critical: it silently notifies shore authorities in the event of an attack, without alerting the ship.
ISPS, güvenliği belirli kişilere atanmış: ISPS embodies security with responsibilities assigned to specific individuals. On board the Ship Security Officer (SSO) is responsible for the implementation of the security plan; On shore, the Company Security Officer (CSO) provides company-level coordination; On the port side, the Port Facility Security Officer (PFSO) manages facility security. This trio ensures uninterrupted security at the ship-port interface. When responsibilities between the ship and the port need to be clarified, a Declaration of Security (DoS) is signed. The security history of the ship is monitored with Continuous Synopsis Record (CSR).
ISPS: gemi güvenlik planının uygulanması: ISPS: the Ship Security Officer (SSO) is responsible for the implementation of the ship security plan; There is CSO on the shore and PFSO in the port.
Several tools complement the operation of ISPS. A Declaration of Security (DoS) is an agreement signed between a ship and a port facility (or another ship) when security responsibilities need to be clarified – for example, if one of the parties is at a higher security level. Continuous Synopsis Record (CSR) ensures identity continuity by tracking the ship's flag, name, owner and class history and is kept on the ship along with the ISSC. Regular drills (typically every three months) and more comprehensive exercises (exercises – annually) are carried out to ensure that the plan does not remain on paper. The system is audited through periodic internal and external verifications and compliance is documented with the International Ship Security Certificate (ISSC). Lack of ISSC or SSP may result in detention at PSC, while security violations may result in denial of admission to the port; In this respect, ISPS is a symmetrical security management system with the safety management of the ISM Code.
ISPS'in operasyonel kalbi üç kademeli gü: The operational heart of ISPS is the three-tier security level system. Level 1 represents normal conditions and includes minimum measures (access control, authentication, patrolling) that are constantly applied. Level 2 comes into play when there is concrete threat intelligence and mandates additional measures (increased search, limited access points). Level 3 applies in extraordinary situations where a security incident is likely or imminent and usually requires special measures coordinated with competent authorities. The flag or port state determines the security level; The ship must immediately adapt to these changes with the procedures defined in its plan.

ISSC (International Ship Security Certificate) is the certificate certifying that a ship has established and implemented security measures within the scope of the ISPS Code. Just as SMC is proof of safety management, ISSC is proof of security (protection against intentional attacks). The certificate is issued by the flag state or an authorized Recognized Security Organization (RSO) after verification that the ship has an approved Ship Security Plan (SSP) and the necessary security equipment. It is valid for five years and undergoes interim verification in the middle of the term.

During the five-year validity cycle, at least one intermediate verification is carried out in the middle of the period, confirming that the ship's security plan is still implemented. For newly built ships or ships changing flag/operator, temporary limited-time ISSC may be issued until full inspection is completed. This structure is symmetrical with the SMC certification logic: one verifies safety management (ISM), the other verifies security management (ISPS), and when both are missing, the ship cannot sail.

ISSC'nin geçerliliği, planın yaşatılması: The validity of the ISSC depends on the survival of the plan. Crews conduct regular safety drills (typically quarterly) and more comprehensive exercises (exercises – annually); These include access control, protection of restricted areas, weapons/explosive threat, stowaways, and transition between the ship's security levels. Security equipment (SSAS, AIS, CCTV, lighting, access control) is tested periodically and records are kept. Preparation for the inspection requires that ship security records (DoS samples, drill records, visitor/cargo security records) are up to date and accessible. Lack of ISSC or approved SSP may lead to detention under PSC inspection, while serious security violations may result in the ship not being accepted to the port; so security is as much a part of the daily operation as safety.

ITC 69, geminin 'büyüklüğünü' parayla ve: ITC 69 translates the 'size' of the ship into a single international language associated with money and safety. There are two basic measures: Gross Tonnage (GT) represents the entire enclosed volume of the ship and forms the basis for regulatory thresholds such as safety requirements, crew numbers, certification types, etc. Net Tonnage (NT) represents only revenue-generating (cargo/passenger) volume and is used in the calculation of commercial cargo such as port fees and canal tolls. The important thing is that these values are volume-based and dimensionless coefficients; It is calculated with the same formula all over the world, unlike inconsistent national systems in the past.
ITC 69, tonajı ölçen idareye göre değişe: ITC 69 transforms tonnage from an estimate that varies depending on the measuring administration into a verifiable mathematical result. Gross tonnage (GT) is calculated by applying a logarithmic coefficient to the ship's total enclosed volume (V, cubic metres): GT = K₁ × V, where K₁ = 0.2 + 0.02 × log₁₀V. The logarithmic coefficient ensures that the contribution of volume to tonnage decreases proportionally in large ships. Net tonnage (NT) represents only revenue-generating (freight/passenger) volume and is calculated with a more complex formula: it includes the parameters cargo volume, draft/depth ratio squared and number of passengers; NT cannot go below certain lower limits. The important thing is that these values are volume-based and dimensionless; Unlike inconsistent national systems in the past (the old Moorsom method), it is calculated with the same formula all over the world and documented with the International Tonnage Certificate.

ITC 69'un pratik önemi, kendi başına bir: The practical importance of ITC 69 lies in the fact that, although it does not establish a safety or environmental rule of its own, it provides the common unit of measurement that determines the scope of almost every IMO convention. A ship learns which articles of these contracts it will be subject to by first looking at the GT value calculated according to ITC 69. For example, the obligation to carry AIS starts at the 300 GT threshold; Many parts of SOLAS for cargo ships (Safety Construction, Safety Equipment certificates) use the 500 GT threshold and MLC 2006 adopts the same 500 GT limit for the Maritime Labor Certificate requirement; The IAPP certification and SOPEP requirement of MARPOL Annex VI is based on a 400 GT threshold, and the EEXI/CII regime increases this threshold to 5000 GT. These thresholds are not arbitrary: they are based on the recognition that the risk posed by large ships, relative to the administrative and technical burden of smaller ships, justifies more severe regulation. Therefore, whether a shipowner keeps GT just below or above a threshold when making a ship design or modification decision is a strategic decision that directly determines which certification and equipment regime it will fall into.

İkinci Mühendis (Second Engineer / 2nd E: As the operational head of the engine room, the Second Engineer is primarily responsible for the daily operation of the main engine, monitoring its performance and early detection of anomalies. This responsibility; It includes daily logging, evaluation of temperature/pressure/rpm/fuel parameters, indicator diagram and PMI (Pressure Measurement Indicator) measurements, cylinder drain oil and scrape-down analysis, scavenge inspection organization and reporting performance monitoring records to the Chief Engineer. This section explains step by step the methodology that the Second Engineer should follow in host machine performance management.
İkinci Mühendis (Second Engineer), makin: The Second Engineer is the day-to-day operational manager of the engine room. He implements the Chief Engineer's directives in the field, manages shift engineers, and is the actual executor of PMS work orders. Daily operation of the main engine, fuel/oil transfers, engine room housekeeping and personnel management are the primary areas of responsibility of this officer. As the most senior officer of the mechanical department after the Chief Engineer, he assumes command of the department in his absence.

Second Engineer is the person who, as the operational head of the engine room, implements the planned maintenance program (PMS - Planned Maintenance System) approved by the Chief Engineer in the field. This responsibility; It includes distributing work orders to shift engineers and machine crews, performing the work correctly/on time/safely, spare parts and consumables management, risk assessment and operation of the permit-to-work system, recording the completed works back to the PMS software and keeping a record chain ready for class/PSC audit. This section explains step by step the methodology that the Second Engineer should follow in maintenance management.
İkinci Mühendis, gemideki yakıt (FO/DO/V: The Second Engineer is responsible for the safe planning and execution of fuel (FO/DO/VLSFO/MGO) and oil (LO) operations on the ship. This task; It covers SOPEP-compliant preparation of the bunker (refueling) operation, scupper closure and drip tray placement, sampling and density/temperature recordings, internal FO/DO transfers, purifier (separator) operation, settling/service tank management and top-up planning with lubricating oil (LO) consumption monitoring. A single bunker operation carried out incorrectly can result in both serious marine pollution penalties and main engine damage due to faulty fuel. This section explains the operation step by step.
İkinci Mühendis, makine dairesi personel: As the operational supervisor of the engine room personnel, the Second Engineer is responsible for establishing the shift order, standardizing shift handover-handover procedures and workforce distribution. This task; It includes preparation of watch bill, management of UMS (non-shift) and traditional shift patterns, keeping overtime and working/rest hours in accordance with MLC 2006 and STCW rules, fatigue management and maintaining discipline/team morale. A properly established shift pattern is a guarantee of both safety and personnel rights. This section explains this management step by step.
İkinci Mühendis, makine dairesinin opera: As the operational head of the engine room, the Second Engineer is primarily responsible for maintaining cleanliness, order and safety standards on a daily basis. Housekeeping; It is not just an aesthetic issue, it is a safety barrier that directly reduces the risks of fire, slip/fall and pollution. Controlling oil leaks, monitoring oil level, keeping lighting working and escape routes clear; These are items directly evaluated in PSC, vetting (SIRE/CDI) and ISM audits. This section explains step by step how the Second Engineer constructed the engine room layout as a management system.

As the operational head of the engine room, the Second Engineer is directly responsible for the maintenance of auxiliary systems—boiler, purifier, and air compressor. Boiler water treatment and safety valve testing, purifier overhaul planning and air compressor valve/cooler maintenance; This ensures the safe and efficient operation of equipment. A boiler safety valve failure or purifier neglect creates both safety and operational risks. This section covers auxiliary system maintenance.

İkinci Zabit (Second Officer / Navigatio: The Second Officer (Navigation Officer) is the main responsible for keeping the paper and electronic charts and all nautical publications on the ship up to date, corrected and ready for the voyage. It keeps the chart portfolio constantly updated with Weekly Notices to Mariners (NtM), T&P (Temporary & Preliminary) notifications, NAVAREA/NAVTEX navigational warnings and ENC (Electronic Navigational Chart) update CD/online services. This section; It explains step by step the weekly NtM application, tracing technique, block correction, chart correction log, ECDIS database update, AIO (Admiralty Information Overlay), folio management, CATZOC/source data reliability and record keeping for PSC audit within the framework of SOLAS V/27 and V/19. Aim; is to set out with a "corrected and approved" map/publication set each time.

The Second Officer (Navigation Officer) is the officer primarily in charge of passage planning / voyage planning on the ship. With berth-to-berth logic, he prepares the plan consisting of four stages — appraisal, planning, execution and monitoring — submits it for the master's approval and monitors the bridge team's implementation. This section explains step by step elements such as route selection, waypoint determination, UKC (Under Keel Clearance) calculation, no-go area identification, contingency anchorage and abort point determination, parallel indexing and squat within the framework of IMO Resolution A.893(21).

The Second Officer (Navigation Officer) is responsible for keeping regular maintenance, testing and calibration records of bridge navigation devices. Gyro compass error and magnetic compass deviation monitoring, speed log calibration, echo sounder checks, RACON/SART tests with radar performance monitor and verification of proper functioning of ECDIS/AIS/VDR form the basis of this task. This section; It explains step by step the navigational equipment requirements of SOLAS Chapter V, IMO performance standards and daily/weekly/voyage control routines. The aim is to ensure that position and maneuver decisions are based on reliable device data and that a complete record is presented in the PSC audit.

Second Officer (Navigation Officer) is the natural owner of practical training that improves the navigational competence of the bridge team as well as navigation planning. Bridge Resource Management (BRM) / Bridge Team Management (BTM) exercises increase the competence of new officers and trainees (cadets) with ship-specific ECDIS familiarization, radar/ARPA training and COLREG scenarios. This section; Within the framework of STCW Manila amendments and IMO type-specific ECDIS training obligation, it explains error chain, challenge & response, closed-loop communication, situational awareness and automation complacency with concrete exercise scenarios. The aim is to transform paper proficiency into real bridge performance.

In the debrief, response time and accuracy are evaluated.
İkinci Zabit, doğu-batı doğrultusunda ya: The Second Officer is responsible for systematically moving the ship's clock forward or backward during east-west voyages and ensuring that this change is consistently reflected in all official records. Clock change; It has a direct impact on the deck logbook, GMDSS radio recording, rest hour charts and ETA calculations and, if mismanaged, can lead to MLC 2006 rest hour violations or loss of recording continuity. This section; It explains step by step the logic of standard time zones and zone description, when and in which shift the time will be changed, keeping the UTC reference constant, retard/advance concepts and international date line transition within the framework of STCW A-VIII/1 and MLC 2006. The Second Officer prepares a clock change plan with the captain's approval, announces it to the crew and ensures that the rest hours are not violated.

This responsibility; This includes performing regular testing of VHF DSC, MF/HF DSC, Inmarsat (FleetBroadband/Fleet One), NAVTEX, EPIRB, SART and portable VHF devices, maintaining a complete GMDSS Radio Log, conducting battery and antenna checks and monitoring spare parts/power supply status. This section; Starting from GMDSS maritime zones (A1-A4), it explains daily/weekly/monthly test procedures, DSC test call logic, distress alert hierarchy and common deficiencies in PSC inspection within the framework of SOLAS Chapter IV.
İkinci Zabit, sefer süresince meteoroloj: The Second Officer is largely responsible for the continuous monitoring and evaluation of the meteorological situation throughout the duration of the voyage. Analysis of NAVTEX, weather fax (radiofax), Inmarsat EGC/SafetyNET weather messages and synoptic maps; Early warning against severe weather conditions, route alternative recommendation and support to the implementation of the heavy weather preparation plan are at the center of this mission. This section; It provides a practical framework from reading pressure systems to weather routing principles, from tropical storm avoidance to ship-specific speed/route decisions. The final route decision always rests with the captain; The Second Officer collects data, analyzes it and prepares a reasoned recommendation.
İkinci Zabit, seyir planlaması ve köprüü: The Second Officer is primarily responsible for navigational planning and bridge operations. Charts, nautical publications, navigational instruments and GMDSS equipment are in the charge of this officer. He works as the bridge's "navigational intelligence": he prepares passage plans, makes meteorological evaluations, follows up ECDIS and radar maintenance, and keeps an active bridge watch in the watch rotation. In accordance with the STCW Code, holding a GMDSS operator certificate is mandatory.
İkinci Zabit, uluslararası pratikte gemi: The Second Officer serves as the ship's medical officer in international practice. In accordance with SOLAS Chapter III and MLC 2006 Rule 4.1, it is mandatory to have adequate medical equipment and medicines on board. Keeping the medical chest inventory up to date, checking the expiration dates of medicines and supplies, keeping the medical log book and preparing supply lists at the port are within the scope of this duty. In case of crew illness or injury, communication with TMAS (Telemedical Assistance Service), patient evaluation and medevac coordination when necessary are carried out by the Second Officer. Organizes medical emergency drills and first aid drills.
İkinci Zabit'in (Second Officer) klasik: The classic shift periods of the Second Officer are 04-08 and 16-20; Since these hours include the transitions between dawn and dusk, they are one of the most critical shifts in terms of navigation. The officer of the watch (OOW), as the master's representative, is independently responsible for the safe navigation of the ship within the framework of the collision avoidance regulations (COLREG 1972) and STCW Code A-VIII/2. This section; It explains step by step the principles of lookout, safe speed, collision risk assessment, radar/ARPA plotting, AIS monitoring, position cross-checking, captain call criteria and Bridge Resource Management (BRM) with the requirements of COLREG Rule 5-19 and STCW. It also addresses the specific risks of the dawn/dusk shift, beacon/shape recognition and sound cues, based on professional practice.
İkinci Zabit'in liderliğinde haftalık VH: Participation in weekly VHF DSC testing, monthly MF/HF DSC testing and portable VHF use in abandon ship drill under the leadership of the Second Officer. İnert gaz iki yoldan üretilir: ya kazan: Inert gas is produced in two ways: either from the flue gas (flue gas, low oxygen) of a boiler or independent burner, or from a nitrogen generator. The flue gas is first washed in a scrubber to remove sulfur and soot particles, and then it is pressed into the tanks with blowers (fans). The system has a critical safety layer that prevents backflow: deck water seal and non-return mechanisms prevent flammable gas in the tank from returning to the engine room; P/V breaker protects the tank from excessive pressure and vacuum. Oxygen analyzers and pressure sensors constantly monitor the system and alarm when limits are exceeded.
İnert gaz ile doldurulmuş tank, oksijens: A tank filled with inert gas is an oxygen-free and potentially toxic confined space. NEVER enter without atmospheric testing, gas freeing and entry permit; Even sticking your head in is fatal.
İnert gaz sistemi (IGS) ile birlikte çal: It is mandatory to work with the inert gas system (IGS); During COW, the tank atmosphere should be kept below 8% O₂ with inert gas.
İnert gaz sistemi farklı amaçlarla, sıkı: The inert gas system is operated in a strict sequence for different purposes: inerting (reducing the oxygen in the tank), purging (diluting flammable vapor by purging it with inert gas), gas-freeing (making the tank safe for human entry by ventilating it), and topping-up (maintaining positive pressure during discharge/cruising). There are critical safety devices that make the system safe: the deck water seal prevents flammable gas from escaping back into the engine room with a liquid barrier, the non-return valve provides an additional backflow barrier, the P/V breaker (pressure/vacuum breaker) protects the tank from excessive pressure and vacuum. Oxygen analyzers and pressure sensors constantly monitor and alarm when limits are exceeded. Inert gas is produced either from boiler/flue gas (washed in a scrubber) or from an independent nitrogen generator; Cargo operation is strictly prohibited when the system is not working and this is a serious finding in both PSC and vetting inspection.
İnert gaz sisteminin en kritik anı, boşa: The most critical moment of the inert gas system is a failure during evacuation: when the pumps are evacuating the tank, if the emptied volume is not replaced by inert gas, an in-tank vacuum will occur and there is a risk of structural collapse (tank implosion); Therefore, in case of IG blower or scrubber failure, it is mandatory to stop the discharge immediately and provide controlled air entry into the tank (only with an approved bypass / vent arrangement). The deck seal is a quiet but vital component of the system; If the water level drops, flammable steam can bypass the deck seal and leak into the fan room, so the water level and heating (to prevent freezing) are checked regularly. In a crude oil washing (COW) operation, the tank is kept in an inert gas atmosphere while simultaneously being washed with high-pressure jets; This dual operation makes oxygen monitoring even more critical because static electricity generated during washing and gases dissolved from sludge layers pose additional risks. This is where crew discipline comes into play: oxygen records are kept every shift, operation is immediately stopped at alarm thresholds, and the cargo operation is never 'temporarily' disabled.
İnert gaz sisteminin tüm amacı, tank atm: The whole purpose of the inert gas system is to keep the tank atmosphere in the zone where combustion is impossible. A hydrocarbon-air mixture can only ignite in the flammable range (between the lower explosion limit LEL and the upper limit UEL); However, when the oxygen content is reduced below a certain threshold, ignition cannot occur regardless of the fuel ratio in the mixture. The inert gas goes below this 'critical dilution line', keeping the tank safe: as a general rule, oxygen is kept below 5% in the pumped inert gas, and below 8% in the tank atmosphere before loading/unloading. The tank is always kept at slightly positive pressure so that no air (and therefore oxygen) leaks in from the outside. This logic explains why continuous oxygen measurement and pressure monitoring are at the heart of the operation.

During loading/unloading the tank is maintained at positive pressure and low oxygen at all times. The crew regularly measures and records the oxygen level, maintains the scrubber/blower, and checks the deck seal water level. It is strictly forbidden to carry out cargo operations when the inert gas system is not working and this is a reason for commercial rejection in PSC detention and vetting (SIRE) inspections.

As long as this force balances the weight of the ship, the ship maintains its buoyancy.

Kapsam yüzdesi geminin seyrettiği güzerg: The percentage of coverage varies depending on the route the ship is on, and it is useful to make this concrete. A voyage from Rotterdam to Hamburg (between two EU ports) is considered intra-EU and all (100%) emissions from the fuel consumed on that voyage are included in the EUA obligation. A voyage from Rotterdam to New York (from an EU port to a non-EU port) is considered extra-EU and only half (50%) of its emissions are covered; The return voyage from New York to Rotterdam is also covered at 50%, the result does not change if the return voyage starts from a non-EU port. In contrast, emissions resulting from the fuel consumed by the ship while it is anchored or berthed (at berth) in the port of Rotterdam are covered 100%, regardless of the voyage route. A voyage from a non-EU port to another non-EU port is completely excluded (0%) because the voyage does not call at an EU port at any point.

The region also hosts heavy dry bulk (especially grain) and tanker traffic; Grain exports from Ukraine and Russia, as well as regional crude oil and product transportation, constantly fill the Black Sea ports. Within the MARPOL framework, there are specific regulations and regional environmental agreements (such as the Bucharest Convention) addressing the environmental sensitivity of the Black Sea; This environmental vulnerability also shapes the control priorities of the Black Sea MoU. Oil log accuracy, ballast water management, waste management plans and operational pollution prevention equipment carry weight in district inspections above the standard PSC scope. For bulk carriers, structural integrity and loading/stacking plans stand out as a special inspection issue because grain cargo carries the risk of slipping into inappropriate stacking.
Karadeniz'e giriş ve çıkış, dünyanın en: Entry and exit to the Black Sea passes through the Turkish Straits (Istanbul and Dardanelles straits), one of the most difficult navigational passages in the world; this is a corridor with heavy traffic, sharp turns and strong currents. Transition requires compliance with the notification and reporting requirements and traffic patterns of the Turkish Straits Vessel Traffic Services (VTS); This is a region where COLREG and navigational safety applications are tested in practice. In terms of PSC, ships must review applicable CIC themes with the crew before entering Black Sea ports, share evidence of finding closure with the flag state and classification society, and take into account their own records in the BS-INFO system where inspection data is shared. The geopolitical dynamics of the region may affect navigation and port access at times; This creates an additional variable in route planning.

Katodik koruma, gövde çeliğinin kendisin: Cathodic protection is based on the principle of sacrificing a metal (zinc or aluminum anode) that is more easily dissolved than the body steel itself and directing corrosion to these anodes; Melting of anodes over time is the normal and expected operating mode of the system. But the rate and pattern of anode consumption is not a mere regeneration schedule but also a diagnostic tool. The melting of all anodes on the body properly and close to the predicted rate indicates that the protection system is working properly. However, melting of anodes in certain areas much faster than expected usually indicates one of two problems: either the coating in that area has deteriorated and the steel has been exposed directly to water, causing the anode to send disproportionate current to that point; Or, there is a stray current on the ship caused by a leaky electrical circuit, and this current consumes the anodes faster than normal. When the surveyor notices this pattern, he not only replaces the anodes but also inspects the coating condition in that area or recommends starting a leakage current survey in the electrical system; Otherwise, they will encounter the same abnormal consumption in the next pool period, or even local corrosion on the underlying steel.

Kısıtlı görüş (restricted visibility), d: Restricted visibility is one of the navigation conditions that causes the most loss of life and property in maritime history. COLREG Rule 19 comes into play when fog, heavy rainfall, snow, sandstorms or other similar conditions restrict visibility. The main difference of Rule 19 from all other rules is that it applies to ships approaching without visual contact and eliminates the give-way / stand-on distinction — each ship must maneuver without having a full view of the opposing ship's position and intentions. While this makes radar reading, ARPA analysis and audio signals critical, it also creates a navigational environment where misinterpretations develop more quickly. For maritime students, all the requirements of Rule 19 — speed, radar, sound signals and maneuvering restrictions — must be understood in their entirety.
Kısıtlı görüş alanında veya yakınında, g: In or near the restricted visibility area, regardless of day or night, the following signs are given at a maximum of 2 minutes apart. Bell/gong is used for ships at anchor and aground.
Kısıtlı görüş koşullarına giren gemi içi: Standard procedures for a ship entering restricted visibility conditions: (1) put engines on standby; (2) start sound signals — motor ship: long blast every 2 minutes (Rule 35(a)); (3) place additional spotters on the bridge and redistribute the workload; (4) light all navigation lights; (5) use radar and ARPA at the highest resolution; (6) Activate AIS and listen to channel 16. Within the scope of GMDSS, NAVTEX fog warnings and announcements on the local port channel should be monitored in the waters in question. SMS (Safety Management System) under ISM requires the ship to document fog procedures in writing; The captain must record in the log book that he followed these procedures.
Kısıtlı görüş koşullarında radar ve ses: In conditions of limited visibility, radar and sound signatures are the two primary means of avoiding conflict. While radar provides target detection and tracking, sound signals provide positional awareness and warning functions at close range. The effective use of these two tools directly determines the level of safety in restricted visibility.

'Selective avoidance' principle: When there is more than one target in ARPA, the maneuver towards the nearest and most dangerous target should not harm the others. Kıyı seyri (Coastal Navigation), geminin:
Coastal navigation is a form of navigation in which the ship navigates within visual distance of the shore or within the scope of radar, and continuous position confirmation can be made. Compared to open sea navigation, it offers more safe reference points and involves more traffic, fewer squares and more danger. This contradictory feature makes coastal navigation techniques both a rich and critical subject.

The essence of coastal navigation techniques lies in the principles of determining a reliable position and ensuring sustainable safety. Instead of adhering to a single method, using visual reference, bearing, transit line, clearing line and electronic systems together creates a reliability hierarchy. When there is an error in one method, the other one steps in and reveals the error; This cross-validation approach should be applied throughout the course.

Radar provides real-time and GPS-independent distance measurement; Detects coastal skyline, pontoons and fixed references. ECDIS, on the other hand, superimposes the electronic map with the GPS location and provides alerting based on dangers.

Klas denetimi süreklidir ve beş yıllık b: Class control is continuous and is established around a five-year cycle. Annual surveys checking the general condition every year, 2-3. An extended interim survey is carried out between the first year and the most comprehensive special survey in the fifth year; this last one usually includes pool inspection. Klas kuruluşları, denizcilik tarihinin e: Classification societies are the oldest risk management institutions in maritime history; It has its origins in London in the 18th century, when merchants and insurers needed to evaluate the condition of ships according to a common measure. Today, a classification society independently verifies that a ship's hull and machinery have been designed, constructed and maintained in accordance with its published technical rules. Being 'in class' means that the ship is considered structurally and mechanically sound; this is effectively mandatory for the validity of insurance, acceptance of the tenant and the basis for flag certificates. Klas sertifikası ile bayrak devleti stat: Class certificates and flag state statute certificates (documents within the scope of SOLAS, MARPOL) are often confused, but they are legally separate systems. Klas verifies, on the basis of a private law contract, that the ship has been structurally and mechanically designed and maintained in accordance with its technical rules; This is not a state authority, but a commercial relationship between the shipowner and the classification society. Statutory compliance, on the other hand, is a public law obligation arising from interstate agreements (SOLAS, MARPOL, MLC) and the final responsibility lies with the flag state. In practice, these two systems overlap to a large extent, as most flag states delegate statute certification to the classification society in the capacity of RO, and the same surveyor carries out both class and statute checks in the same visit. However, the overlap is not complete: even if a ship is in class, a deficiency in purely operational/administrative areas such as ISM, ISPS or MLC does not fall within the scope of class and is recorded as a separate deficiency in the PSC. Conversely, class loss automatically becomes a PSC retention because the validity of statute certificates is often dependent on class approval. Therefore, saying 'it has a class certificate' does not mean 'there is full status compliance'; The two are parallel but legally independent layers of assurance.

Trimming (even distribution of the load within the hold) is critical for both stability and structural load distribution. Some loads require closed ventilation (to avoid reaction with oxygen), while others require constant ventilation and gas metering because they can accumulate toxic/flammable gas. During loading, the crew monitors the visual condition of the cargo (signs of moisture, water infiltration) and stops the operation in case of doubt. Grain is separate from this code and is regulated by a separate Grain Code.
Kod, gemileri buzda çalışma kabiliyetine: The code categorizes ships according to their ability to operate in ice: Category A operates in the harshest ice conditions (Polar Class PC1-5), Category B operates in thinner ice (PC6-7), and Category C operates in open waters that do not require ice reinforcement. Polar Class indicates how reinforced the ship's hull is. Every ship carries two critical documents: the Polar Ship Certificate, which demonstrates ice navigation competence, and the Polar Water Operational Manual (PWOM), which includes route-specific ice/weather conditions, SAR coverage, communications and escape plan. PWOM is the captain's operational compass that predefines how he will act under which conditions in the pole.

Kodun teknik özü, tahıl kaymasından doğa: The technical essence of the code is to calculate the heeling moment resulting from grain shifting and prove that the ship's stability reserve is sufficient against this. The calculation is made with different space assumptions for partially filled and fully filled warehouses. Konşimento (Bill of Lading, B/L) üç teme: The Bill of Lading (B/L) serves three basic functions: (1) Receipt — is evidence that the cargo has been received on board the ship in the quantity and condition specified; (2) Evidence of the contract of carriage—reflects the terms between the carrier and the cargo party; (3) Negotiable instrument / document of title - transfer of the bill of lading means the transfer of ownership of the cargo and the cargo is received by presenting the bill of lading. This triple function places the bill of lading at the center of international trade and letters of credit payments.

There are also 'shipped/on board' (confirming that the cargo has been loaded onto the ship) and 'received for shipment' bills of lading. A 'clean' bill of lading does not contain any visible damage/deficiency in the cargo; Registered (dirty) bill of lading carries a damage notice and creates problems in the letter of credit.
