UNCLOS Article 105 recognizes the power of a warship or authorized state ship on the high seas to intercept, board, seize, and arrest persons on board a pirate ship; This authority stems from the fact that piracy is a crime subject to universal jurisdiction, meaning that every state has the right to prosecute it, regardless of which state's flag it flies. SUA expands this framework: even if an incident does not fall within the classical definition of piracy (on the high seas, for private benefit), if it constitutes a crime within the scope of SUA (seizing a ship, violence against crew, endangering the safety of navigation), Article 8bis boarding procedures of the 2005 Protocol come into play and the suspect ship can be boarded with the permission of the flag state. International naval force operations in the Gulf of Aden and off the coast of Somalia (such as Combined Task Force 151, EU NAVFOR Atalanta) in practice rely precisely on the combination of these two legal foundations (UNCLOS Article 105 piracy jurisdiction and SUA criminal definitions); Suspects caught are usually prosecuted under SUA or national piracy legislation in a party state in the region.

'Minimum safe shift personnel' regulated under STCW Rule VIII/2 and the bridge organization determined within the framework of the IMO MSC Circular constitute the legal basis for workload management. Procedurally, critical tasks are shared to avoid ‘single point failure’: the officer monitoring the navigation chart and the officer monitoring VHF traffic must be different people. In this case, each ship slows down to a safe speed, keeps the machines ready for maneuver and makes systematic observations with radar. When maneuvering against a ship detected solely by radar, two behaviors should be avoided: turning to port to a ship ahead of oneself (other than ahead) and changing course to approach a ship in cabin/sideline or astern of oneself. This article also envisages the profile of a captain who evaluates and judges the situation in its entirety rather than blindly following the rules. Although COLREG rules give clear instructions for certain situations (crossing, head-on, overtaking), it is not possible to foresee all scenarios in the open sea; Rule 2 closes this loophole. In practice, the concept of 'good maritime practice' is widely used in court decisions: what would a reasonable captain do in these circumstances? Internalizing this standard provides a much more permanent professional competence than memorizing the rules.

Leeway (wind drift) is the phenomenon in which the actual path (COG - Course Over Ground) followed by the ship, under the influence of wind force, deviates towards the leeward from the route indicated by the ship's heading. In other words: although the ship steers in a certain direction, the wind pushes it laterally and the actual track deviates from the intended course.

LLC'nin 1988 Protokolü, sözleşmenin dene: The 1988 Protocol of the LLC introduces the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification (HSSC), which puts the audit architecture of the convention on the same schedule as SOLAS and MARPOL. Before the protocol, since each contract had its own survey and certificate renewal cycle, a ship might have to receive more than one inspection visit on different dates in the same year. The HSSC and Load Line Certificate also fall into a common five-year certification cycle and annual/periodic surveys can be scheduled to coincide with the windows of SOLAS's Safety Construction and Safety Equipment surveys and MARPOL's IOPP/IAPP surveys (usually ±3 months of the main date). In this way, the classification society can check the ship's watertightness, structural integrity and pollution prevention equipment together in a single survey visit. The protocol also standardized the display of the free board mark and tonnage marks on the certificate and strengthened the certificate recognition between state parties. In practice, this means that survey planning for ship management should not be considered separately LLC but within a single annual program together with the SOLAS and MARPOL survey schedule.

LRIT (Long-Range Identification and Tracking) is a system established within the scope of SOLAS for remote identification and tracking of ships on a global scale. While AIS is a local/in-range broadcast system, LRIT transmits a ship's identity and location via satellite as a closed (secret) data stream to authorized states. In this respect, LRIT differs from open broadcast AIS in terms of both purpose and privacy.

Standard reporting typically occurs several times per day (e.g., every 6 hours); However, data centers can remotely increase the reporting frequency or request location information instantly (on-demand polling) according to the request of the monitoring state. This flexibility allows for more frequent tracking when a ship approaches a certain area or in a special situation. Unlike AIS, LRIT data is not publicly available; only authorized parties can access.

LRIT ile AIS sıkça karıştırılır ancak fa: LRIT and AIS are often confused, but they solve different problems. AIS broadcasts locally and openly over VHF; its range is limited to the radio horizon and its primary purpose is conflict avoidance and local situational awareness (anyone can listen). LRIT, on the other hand, provides global coverage via satellite, produces less frequent reports, and its data is confidential/available only to authorized states. In summary, AIS is for 'ships to see each other'; LRIT is for 'states to monitor ships remotely'. The two do not replace each other, they complement each other.

Which ship data a state can access is regulated according to the Data Distribution Plan (DDP) determined by IMO; Thus, each state only has access to the data of ships flying its own flag, approaching its coast or coming to its port.

Makine Stajyeri (Engine Cadet), denizcil: Engine Cadet is a candidate engineer who is on a ship to complete the marine internship part of maritime training in the mechanical department. By completing the sea service period stipulated by the STCW Code, he/she receives practical training on the way to Shift Engineer qualification. The intern has no authority or signature responsibility on board; however, he/she is expected to participate in all machine operations at an observation and support level. Training Record Book (TRB) is the official document of this process.
Makine stajyeri (Engine Cadet), STCW Böl: The Engine Cadet participates in engine room duty under the direct supervision of the Engineer Officer of the Watch (EOOW) to gain STCW Part A-III/1 competency areas practically on the ship. This participation; Includes parameter reading, log book recording, liquid level control, alarm recognition, engine room round routine and teamwork. The intern has no authority to make independent decisions or keep independent shifts; Every intervention, every switching and every unusual situation is made with EOOW approval. This section explains step by step the methodology, regulatory framework and safety limits that the trainee must follow in supervised shift participation.
Makine stajyeri, gemide geçirdiği her se: The mechanical intern must document each sailing period he spends on the ship with an official Sea Service Certificate signed by the captain. This document is the main evidence in proving the period of sea service required for STCW's OOW (Officer of the Watch — Machinery) qualification certificate. In addition, obtaining a Watchkeeping Certificate for the Engine Department requires that all competency areas within the scope of STCW Table A-III/1 be completed in TRB and approved by the instructor engineer. Loss or irregularity of documents may mean that the internship period is not recognized or the examination right is postponed. This section explains step by step the structure of the Sea Service document, the sea service account, the certification process and document management.

Makine stajyeri, gemideki acil sistemler: The mechanical trainee must learn the operation and test procedures of the emergency systems on the ship as an observer. These systems; It covers emergency generator, emergency fire pump, emergency air compressor and emergency steering gear tests. The intern also learns the remote operation principles of quick closing valve, emergency stop and ventilation flaps, and how to follow the blackout recovery procedure step by step. These systems are the last line of defense to maintain the safety of the ship when normal power and control are lost. This section describes each system's function, testing logic, and regulatory requirement.
Makine stajyeri, gemideki sistemleri anl: The mechanical trainee must gain two key skills to understand the shipboard systems and manage maintenance: reading technical drawings and using Planned Maintenance System (PMS) software. Technical drawings; It provides a "map" of the system with documents such as piping diagram, electrical diagram and general arrangement. PMS is the digital core of maintenance work planning, work order opening/closing, spare parts coding and stock control. This chapter explains the drawing reading methodology, symbols, and PMS workflow step by step.
Makine stajyeri, geminin can damarı olan: The mechanical trainee must practically learn the fuel oil and lubricating oil systems, which are the lifeblood of the ship. This learning; It includes supervised monitoring of bunker (fuel supply) operation, FO/DO settling and service tank systems, purifier (separator) operation, LO sump and circulation circuit. The intern also learns fuel/oil sampling, observation of viscosity and density measurement, and the logic of filling by reading the Oil Record Book (ORB) Part I format. These systems are critical for both the reliability of the machine and the prevention of marine pollution within the scope of MARPOL. This section explains step by step the operation of the systems, control points and regulatory requirements.
Makine stajyeri, makine dairesinin yükse: The mechanical trainee must systematically learn basic safety procedures in order to work safely in the high-risk environment of the engine room. These procedures; It includes energy isolation (LOTO - Lockout/Tagout), work permit system (PTW - Permit to Work), enclosed space entry, hot work and personal protective equipment (PPE) use. In addition, the intern; Learns emergency procedures such as blackout rescue, engine room fire and flooding, escape routes and muster station information and actively participates in drills. This chapter explains step by step the rationale for each safety procedure, its regulatory basis and the trainee's role in practice.
Makine stajyeri, pompa overhaul, valf ba: The machine intern participates as an assistant in maintenance work such as pump overhaul, valve maintenance, filter replacement, gasket cutting, heat exchanger cleaning and bolt torqueing. The purpose of this participation is; learning the names and functions of equipment parts, gaining correct tool use and dexterity, becoming familiar with the technical language and experiencing the safe conduct of maintenance work. The intern does not carry out care independently; Works within the scope of work order and permit under the supervision of the responsible engineer or experienced oiler/fitter. This section details the methods, safety steps and learning strategy that the trainee should follow in care support.

MARPOL'ü anlamanın anahtarı, onu tek bir: The key to understanding MARPOL is to view it not as a single set of rules but as a collection of six annexes, each targeting a different type of pollutant. Annex I regulates oil, Annex II harmful liquid chemicals, Annex III packaged hazardous substances, Annex IV sewage, Annex V litter, and Annex VI air emissions. Some or all of these annexes apply depending on a ship type and the cargo it carries. The common logic of the contract is to combine 'discharge standard' with 'equipment/recording obligation': how much can be discharged, where and under what conditions is defined by numerical limits; The hardware that provides this (OWS, purification unit, scrubber) and the records proving this (ORB, Garbage Record Book) are required.

Metasentrik nokta, geminin küçük yatma a: The metacentric point is one of the basic geometric reference points used to define the stability behavior of the ship under small heel angles. When the ship is upright, the direction of the buoyant force is represented by a vertical line passing through the center of buoyancy. When the ship tilts at a very small angle, the center of buoyancy shifts to a new position and the direction of buoyancy passing through this new point intersects with the initial direction at a point. This intersection point is called the metacentric point and is usually denoted by the letter M.
Metasentrik nokta, yalnızca küçük yatma: The metacentric point is a concept that is valid only for small angles of repose and is therefore used in “initial stability” or “small angles stability” analyses. As the angle of repose increases, the path followed by the center of lift ceases to be linear and the metacentric approach loses its validity. The metacentric point therefore defines the initial heeling behavior of the ship, not the large angles stability.

Metasentrik yüksekliğin büyüklüğü, gemin: The size of the metacentric height also determines the movement character of the ship. Ships with very large GM values are called “hard” ships; These ships make fast and short-term rolling movements. This may increase structural loads and negatively affect personnel comfort. In contrast, ships with very small GM values are defined as “soft” ships; Periods of roll are long and the ship exhibits slow, reluctant movements. Excessively small GM values bring the risk of loss of stability.

This distance directly determines whether the ship will behave stable or unstable at a small angle of heel. When the metacentric height is positive, the metacentric point is located above the center of gravity and the ship is considered stable. When the metacentric height is zero, the center of gravity and the metacentric point coincide and the ship is in indifferent equilibrium. When the metacentric height is negative, the metacentric point remains below the center of gravity and the ship behaves unstable.

MF ve düşük HF'te sinyal büyük ölçüde 'y: In MF and low HF, the signal propagates largely by following the earth as a 'ground wave'; MF ground wave gives a typical range of 100–150 nautical miles during the day, greater at night. At higher frequencies the 'sky wave' predominates: the wave reaches the ionosphere, refracts back to earth and can reach thousands of miles away. A 'skip zone' may occur between the place where the ground wave ends and the place where the first sky wave bounce falls, where the signal cannot be received. As the ionosphere changes with day/night, season, and solar activity, the available frequencies also change.

MLC 2006, beş Title etrafında örgütlenir: MLC 2006 is organized around five Titles, each securing a different dimension of the seafarer's life. Title 1 establishes the minimum conditions for work on board: minimum age (16, with stricter limits for night and hazardous work), valid health certificate, vocational training and regulated recruitment/placement services. Title 2 covers the conditions of employment: written Maritime Employment Agreement (SEA), regular wage payment, working/rest hours, leave entitlement and repatriation. Title 3 governs the fact that the ship is a living space: cabin, ventilation, lighting, dining and recreation standards. Title 4 covers health protection, medical care, occupational safety and social security. Title 5 regulates compliance and implementation (certification, audit, complaint mechanisms). Each Title consists of binding Standards (Part A) and guiding Guidelines (Part B).
MLC 2006, denizcilerin onurlu ve adil ko: MLC 2006 provides for seafarers to work in dignified and fair conditions. The D&A process must be conducted in accordance with the principles of confidentiality, registration and fair consideration, even while applying zero tolerance; Otherwise, it creates both legal and reputational risks.
MLC 2006, gıda/catering dahil yaşam koşu: MLC 2006 provides for complaints mechanisms and regular inspections of living conditions, including food/catering. Satisfaction tracking is the practical tool of this well-being framework.
MLC 2006, gıdanın besin değeri açısından: MLC 2006 also requires food to be sufficient in terms of nutritional value. A balanced, micronutrient-sustainable menu is the core of the chef's health contribution.
MLC 2006, gıdanın yeterli miktar, besin: MLC 2006 requires food to be provided in sufficient quantity, nutritional value, quality and variety and free of charge. Budget discipline is no excuse for lowering this standard; the cook balances the two together.
MLC 2006, mürettebata yeterli ve güvenli: MLC 2006 requires crews to be provided with adequate and safe drinking water; Water quality should be monitored and hygiene records kept.
MLC 2006, SOLAS, MARPOL ve STCW'nin yanı: MLC 2006 sits alongside SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW as the 'fourth pillar' of maritime law; because while the former regulate the ship and professional qualifications, the MLC directly protects the humane working and living conditions of the seafarer. It combines 68 separate conventions and recommendations within the ILO into a single consolidated text. Its structure is built around five Titles, and each Title consists of binding Standards (Part A) and guiding Guidelines (Part B). The strength of the convention comes from the principle of 'no more favorable treatment', which subjects a ship to both flag state inspection and port state control: even a ship of a flag that has not ratified the MLC is inspected in an MLC member port.
MLC 2006: maksimum 14 saat/24 saatlik pe: MLC 2006: operation in a maximum 14 hour/24 hour period or 72 hour/7 day period.
MLC 2006'nın tasarımında bilinçli bir es: There is deliberate flexibility in the design of the MLC 2006: rather than imposing the same rigid pattern on each country's legal system, administrative structure and existing legislation, the convention allows different means of implementation that achieve the same protective goal. This is called 'substantial equivalence' and is embodied in DMLC Part I. For example, a standard may stipulate a certain minimum square footage of seafarer accommodation; Instead of strictly applying this minimum square metre, a country may adopt an alternative regulation (e.g. a different space-to-person ratio, additional common space compensation) adapted to its ship types and climatic conditions, but which equally protects the seafarer's overall quality of life and privacy; This is conditioned on the ILO being informed of the justification for this difference and demonstrating that the alternative provides 'exactly equal' protection of the standard. This flexibility is an important reason why the MLC has been able to bring more than 100 flag states around the world with different legal and shipbuilding traditions into the same contract; A rigid, one-dimensional set of standards would not find such broad acceptance.
MLC Certificate (Maritime Labour Certifi: MLC Certificate (Maritime Labor Certificate) is a certificate that certifies that a ship meets the working and living conditions standards within the scope of MLC 2006. While SOLAS certificates document the ship and STCW document the competence of the crew, the MLC Certificate directly ensures the humane working conditions of the seafarer. Mandatory for international expedition ships of 500 GT and above; It is issued by the flag state or authorized classification society after compliance with the 14 MLC control areas is verified. It is valid for five years and is subject to an interim audit in the middle of the term.

MLC sertifikasyonunda en sık denetlenen: The most frequently inspected and most frequently deficient area in MLC certification is working/rest hours. The rule applies with a limit of either maximum work (maximum 14 hours in 24 hours, maximum 72 hours in 7 days) or minimum rest (minimum 10 hours in 24 hours, minimum 77 hours in 7 days); The rest can be divided into two parts at most and one part should be at least 6 hours. These hours are recorded daily for each sailor and a copy is given to the sailor. It is essential that the records reflect reality: records that appear compliant on paper but actually conceal overwork are violations of both MLC and STCW and have serious consequences in the PSC audit. These rules closely match the fatigue provisions of the STCW; because fatigue is both a seafarer's right issue and a direct safety risk.

MLC, gemide ayrımcılığı yasaklar, adil ç: MLC prohibits discrimination on board, ensures fair working conditions and an on-board complaints procedure. MLC, liman devleti kontrolünde en sık ek: MLC is one of the areas where port state control is most frequently lacking; because problems such as unpaid wages, overwork, insufficient food or poor accommodation are concrete and easily identified. Serious MLC violations may lead to detention of the ship. Additionally, the MLC gives the seafarer direct power: through grievance mechanisms onboard and ashore, a seafarer can mobilize the port state and this can trigger an inspection. That's why ships keep DMLC Part II up to date, keep working hour records regularly and are always prepared for PSC MLC inspections.
MLC, mürettebata temiz, hijyenik ve sağl: The MLC requires crew to be provided with clean, hygienic and healthy living conditions. Bathroom/toilet hygiene, ventilation and sanitation are supervised by the PSC.
MLC'nin denizciyi en somut biçimde koruy: One of the provisions of the MLC that most concretely protects seafarers is the right to repatriation and the mandatory financial security that supports it. A seafarer must be returned to his country free of charge when his contract ends, he becomes ill, or the ship/company cannot fulfill its obligations. The financial security added by the 2014 amendments (usually through P&I insurance) comes into play in the event of shipowner bankruptcy or seafarer abandonment: it covers outstanding wages, repatriation costs and basic needs. The ship is required to keep certificates showing this financial assurance (e.g. separate documents for abandonment and death/long-term disability) visible on board; Their absence will result in a deficiency record in the PSC audit. This mechanism is a response to past cases where seafarers were left unpaid and helpless in foreign ports for months.
MLC'nin gücü, denetlenebilir olmasından: The power of MLC comes from its auditability. International expedition ships of 500 GT and above must carry a Maritime Labor Certificate issued by the flag state and a two-part DMLC (Part I indicates state requirements, Part II indicates company measures); These are valid for five years and are subject to interim audit. The principle that strengthens the scope of the agreement is 'no more favorable treatment': even a ship of a flag that has not ratified the MLC is inspected in an MLC member port, so that substandard operators cannot take advantage. Grievance mechanisms that give direct power to the seafarer operate both on board and ashore and are protected against retaliation; A seafarer can trigger an inspection by reporting unpaid wages or poor conditions to the port state. The MLC is one of the most frequent areas of deficiencies in port state control, with serious violations leading to ship detention; Mandatory financial security added by the 2014 amendments comes into play in the event of bankruptcy of the shipowner or abandonment of the seafarer.

Monitoring (İzleme), passage planning sü:
Monitoring is the final phase of the passage planning process and continues throughout the journey. At this stage, the compliance of the navigation plan with the actual application conditions is regularly checked; When deviations are detected, the reasons are investigated and necessary corrective measures are taken. Monitoring is not a reactive alarm management; It is a proactive compliance monitoring process.

The effectiveness of monitoring is directly related to the situational awareness of the bridge team. The officer who notices the deviation must understand its cause (current, wind, loss of speed, aiming error?), assess its extent, and take appropriate corrective action in a timely manner.
Monitoring kapsamındaki temel parametrel: Basic parameters within the scope of monitoring: (1) Position: GPS COG and position; It is verified at regular intervals by radar fix or visual confirmation. Position updates are made hourly in the open sea and frequently on the shore. (2) XTE: Instantly monitored on ECDIS; intervention occurs when the alarm threshold is exceeded. (3) SOG and ETA: Compared with planned speed and arrival time; Significant deviations require updating. (4) Meteorology: Barometer trend, visual observations and NAVTEX/SafetyNET messages are compared to plan expectations.
Monitoring sırasında tespit edilen bir s: A deviation detected during monitoring is handled through a systematic process: (1) Detect the deviation and measure its size (XTE amount, ETA difference, speed difference). (2) Recognize the cause: is the discharge stronger than expected? Is the wind in an unplanned direction? Loss of speed due to machine problem? (3) Determine corrective action: heading correction, speed adjustment or plan revision. (4) Inform the captain if necessary. (5) Save to log.

Occlusion occurs when the cold front catches up with the warm front and the warm sector breaks away from the surface. There are two types: cold occlusion (the air behind is colder) and warm occlusion (the air behind is relatively warmer). Occluded fronts produce complex weather conditions; Both cold and warm front features can be observed together. Stationary front is a front that has no significant movement and is in balance between two masses. Olgunlaşmış bir tropikal siklon, merkezd: A mature tropical cyclone consists of three main structural regions from the center outward. In the center is the eye, where the lowest pressure of the system is measured, the wind weakens and the sky can partially clear; Its typical diameter varies between 20–60 km. OPRC metninin kendisi 'Tier 1/2/3' terim: The OPRC text itself does not use the term 'Tier 1/2/3', but the structure that the convention imposes on national emergency plans is commonly applied in the industry with this tiered logic. At the lowest level are small-scale leaks that the ship can respond to with its own SOPEP equipment (limited amounts of sorbents, booms and dispersants); At this stage, intervention is initiated by the ship crew within minutes. When a spill exceeds the ship's own capacity, larger volume booms, recovery vessels and storage units in regional stockpile centers (held by port operators, national coastal protection agencies or industry consortiums) come into play; This level can reach the field within hours. In the largest-scale events (such as a major tanker accident), national capacity may also be insufficient and the international mutual aid mechanisms envisaged by the OPRC will be activated; This involves other states sending expert teams, specialized equipment, and even response ships to the scene. National emergency plans pre-define the transition thresholds and trigger decisions between these three levels.
OPRC-HNS Protokolü'nün pratikte petrol s: The point where the OPRC-HNS Protocol differs from oil spill response in practice is that the physical and toxicological behavior of hazardous and harmful substances (cargoes such as acids, solvents, liquefied gas carried by chemical tankers) is very different from oil. While oil can spread on the water surface and be surrounded by the boom, some HNS substances dissolve in water, sink, evaporate, or react with water to release toxic gas; This makes standard boom and sorbent equipment often useless. HNS response therefore requires different equipment and expertise: vapor suppression systems, chemical-specific personal protective equipment (at a much higher level of protection than the standard oil response suit), gas detectors and substance-specific neutralization agents. Due to the cost and infrequent use of this specialized capacity, a significant portion of the world's ports do not have HNS response capacity, although they are proficient in oil spill response; This gap requires shipowners operating chemical tankers to investigate in advance which ports can offer real HNS response support in route planning.
OPRC'nin gemi düzeyindeki somut çıktısı,: The tangible output of the OPRC at the ship level is the emergency response plan that every ship carries: SOPEP for oil and SMPEP, its integrated version combining oil and hazardous materials. These plans describe step-by-step who will do what, which valve to close, where the equipment is located, and who to call in the event of a leak. Notification is vital: a pollution incident must be reported immediately to the nearest coastal state, in a standard format (pollution type, estimated quantity, weather/sea conditions, actions taken); Early notification enables response resources to be mobilized in a timely manner.

GHG Fuel Standard, on the other hand, directly imposes a technical limit on the density of the fuel (similar logic to FuelEU) and imposes a forced technical transition instead of a price signal; While it provides flexibility for fleets with long distance, irregular traffic, it can pose operational risks for shipowners operating in regions with low alternative fuel availability. The chief officer does not assign tanks without checking this chart when making a new loading plan, because the mixing of two incompatible substances through leakage, faulty valve operation, or a common drain line can lead to a violent exothermic reaction, outgassing, or polymerization. Many of the reactive cargo accidents experienced in industry have resulted from precisely this type of unexpected mixing: seemingly minor operational errors, such as the leakage of residue from one tank into a neighboring tank, the diversion of wash water into the wrong line, or the mixing of vapors in the common vent system, have resulted in uncontrolled pressure increases or the formation of a toxic gas cloud. Paralel indeks (Parallel Index), radar v:
Parallel Index is a navigation tracking technique that plots parallel to the planned course line on the radar or ECDIS and continuously shows the horizontal distance between the ship and a fixed reference point (usually a prominent shore point, cape, lighthouse or radar reflector). The technique is very simple in essence: the ship's distance to a certain point is kept under control at all times by drawing a line parallel to the course line according to the position of that point on the radar or ECDIS screen.

The parallel index is one of the most critical navigation tools of the bridge, especially in narrow straits, approach routes of ports, shallow waters and situations where visibility is limited. Thanks to this technique, the officer can instantly see how much he has deviated from the planned route; Small deviations can interfere before they become larger. The fact that it can be applied with radar, even without a visual cue or if the GPS is corrupted, increases the reliability of the technique.

Parallel index implementation is based on the principle that the only truly useful cruise control is instantaneous, continuous, and visual verification. Just knowing the ship's location is not enough; It is necessary to make sure that the ship is moving in the right direction and at the right distance. Therefore, IMO and STCW legislation define the parallel index technique as a mandatory component of bridge qualification programmes.

(3) During navigation, the reflection of the reference point is detected on the screen and the PI line is adjusted to show that reflection. (4) If the reference point lags behind the line, the ship is moving away from the planned route; If it's in front of you, it means it's getting closer.

Paris MoU, liman devleti kontrolünün böl: The Paris MoU is the memorandum of understanding that invented regional coordination of port state control and became a model for the world. A single state's controls cover only its own ports; but ships operate regionally. The basic idea of the Paris MoU is that member states share audit results in a common database (THETIS) and divide the audit burden among them. Thus, when a ship is inspected in a member port, the result is visible to all members and substandard ships can be tracked throughout the region while unnecessary re-inspections are avoided. It covers one of the busiest maritime traffic regions in the world, with 27 member states.
Paris MoU'nun 2011'de uygulamaya koyduğu: The New Inspection Regime (NIR), introduced by the Paris MoU in 2011, forms the backbone of the modern PSC. To every ship; A risk profile is assigned based on type, age, flag performance, class (RO) performance, past inspection results and ISM/ISPS history. The ship is considered High (HRS), Standard (SRS) or Low (LRS) risk and inspection frequency is determined accordingly: high-risk ships are targeted every few months, low-risk ones every two to three years. In addition, Concentrated Inspection Campaigns (CIC) are conducted once or twice a year, focusing on a specific issue (e.g. BWM, STCW, fire safety).
Paris MoU'nun operasyonel beyni THETIS a: The operational brain of the Paris MoU is the information system called THETIS: the results of inspections at all member ports, ship risk profiles, detected deficiencies and detention records are collected in this central database and shared in real time. The system calculates which ship should be inspected based on its risk profile and provides target lists to inspectors; thus, audit effort is directed at the risk most. Each detected deficiency is recorded with standardized codes (17 main categories and hundreds of sub-codes) and an action is assigned to it. Thanks to this coding, a finding in one port becomes visible in another member port; A deficiency that needs to be corrected at the next port can be tracked and recurring findings can be revealed. THETIS is also integrated with the EU PSC Directive as THETIS-EU for EU member ports.
Paris MOU'nun risk endeksi; bayrak, sını: Risk index of Paris MOU; It is calculated based on flag, classification society, number of previous detentions and age.
Paris MoU'nun risk hedeflemesi yalnızca: The Paris MoU's risk targeting evaluates not only the ship but also the actors behind it. Flag state performance (White/Grey/Black list) as well as past performance of the ship operating company and the recognized organization (RO) that classifies the ship also enter into the risk profile: an operator or classification society that has caused a large number of detentions or deficiencies will have its ships inspected more frequently. This creates deterrence that spreads liability from a single ship across the entire fleet and service chain; Substandard management also becomes commercially expensive. Good performance is rewarded: ships reaching the low-risk profile (LRS) are inspected less frequently and the priority window is widened. Thus, the Paris MoU establishes a continuous quality pressure throughout the sector, beyond individual inspections.
The enforcement power of the Paris MoU is gradual. Serious deficiencies lead to detention of the ship; Repeated detentions lead to a ban—three detentions for three months, a fourth for twelve months, a fifth for twenty-four months, and then a permanent ban. Inspection performance also affects flag states: flags are divided into White, Gray and Black lists based on their three-year retention rates, and this ranking determines the likelihood of that flag's ships being inspected. Ships therefore monitor their risk profiles via THETIS, prepare for CIC themes and close deficiencies in advance.
Paris ve Tokyo MOU çerçevesinde armatör/: Within the framework of the Paris and Tokyo MOU, the shipowner/operator has the right to review/appeal to the port state against a detention decision. The objection does not automatically lift the detention; However, if it is found to be unfair, the record will be corrected. The captain must collect all the evidence (photographs, records, survey reports) that will be the basis for the objection from the first moment.

Passage planning (route / voyage planning) is the comprehensive preparation process carried out before the cruise to ensure that the ship reaches the destination from the departure point safely, efficiently and in accordance with the legislation. IMO Resolution A.893(21) divides this process into four mandatory stages: Appraisal, Planning, Execution and Monitoring. This framework is also supported by SOLAS Chapter V; It creates a legal liability on the captain and navigation officers of all ships operating internationally.

The importance of route planning stems from the fact that it enables the bridge to operate 'proactively' rather than 'reactively' by identifying hazards and constraints in advance. When navigating without a plan, dangers are noticed as they approach; In these moments, both time and space for movement are limited. PDOP (Position Dilution of Precision) refers to the total geometric precision dilution in both horizontal and vertical position components of the GNSS receiver. PDOP is equal to the square root of the sum of the squares of HDOP and VDOP:

PDOP = √(HDOP² + VDOP²)

This relationship clearly shows that PDOP is always greater than or equal to HDOP; because when vertical uncertainty is added, the total position uncertainty increases. In marine navigation, PDOP provides an overview of 3D position accuracy; however, HDOP is often the primary monitoring parameter.

Processes such as high-speed loading, splash filling, and filter/mixing accumulate static charge; ISGOTT therefore defines measures such as low flow at startup, prevention of splashing, bonding of equipment and specific waiting times. Gas danger arises from the mixture of cargo vapor with air being in the flammable range (between LEL and UEL). ISGOTT aims to keep the tank atmosphere outside this dangerous range: the most common method is to reduce oxygen with an inert gas system below the level at which combustion is impossible (the general rule is 8%) and keep the tank at positive pressure. Polar Code, buzlu sularda seyrin sıradan: The Polar Code arises from the fact that navigation in icy waters is radically different from ordinary sailing. In polar regions, ships face ice burdens, extremely low temperatures, long dark periods, limited mapping, poor communications and isolation where the nearest help can be days away. While an accident might be manageable in temperate waters, it could be fatal in the arctic. The Code therefore combines both safety (SOLAS Chapter
Polar Code, gemileri buzla başa çıkma ka: The Polar Code rates ships into seven Polar Classes (PC1-PC7) based on their ability to deal with ice; this is based on the IACS Unified Requirements. PC1 can operate year-round in the thickest perennial ice in all polar waters, while PC7 can only operate in thin first-year ice in summer. Higher classes require thicker hull sheet metal, reinforced frame structure, ice-reinforced propeller and rudder, and low-temperature steel. This classification combines ship categories: Category A operates in the harshest conditions (PC1-5), Category B operates in thinner ice (PC6-7), and Category C operates in open waters that do not require ice reinforcement. A ship may only sail in the ice and temperature conditions specified in its Polar Ship Certificate; This concretely limits which area the captain can enter and under what circumstances.

Pratikte tahıl yükleme kararı tek kişini: In practice, the decision to load grain is not the product of a single person, but of a pre-established approval chain. The ship's classification society or flag state approves a grain loading booklet containing stability calculations specific to the ship's geometry (hatch shape, longitudinal bulkheads, tank layout) and issues a Document of Authorization based on this; This document predefines under what occupancy conditions (fully loaded, partially loaded, feeding applied) the ship can safely carry grain. Before loading, the chief officer calculates the overturning moment and residual stability by comparing the planned loading case with the reference cases in the booklet; This calculation is usually independently verified before the payload layout is agreed with the terminal, as even a small deviation from a reference case in the booklet can exceed the criteria. Loading grain without a valid Document of Authorization or booklet account specific to that voyage is unacceptable both commercially and legally: the port authority and P&I insurers may reject such loading, the flag state may open an investigation, and the ship may be detained under PSC supervision. Undocumented or unaccounted loading means taking grain to sea without knowing its true behavior, which directly defeats the Grain Code's raison d'être.

PSC denetçisinin gözünde DMLC Part I ile: DMLC Part I and Part II have very different weight in the eyes of the PSC auditor. Part I is essentially a summary of the flag state's national legislation; It does not carry any new information for the auditor, because that legislation is already public and the auditor relies on the flag state to verify it. Part II has a completely different nature: it is a commitment in which the company writes in its own voice, 'we meet these requirements concretely with these procedures, this recording system, these responsible persons'. This commitment translates directly into a testable checklist in the auditor's hands: if Part II says 'working hours are logged with the following software', the auditor requests records of that software; If it says 'complaints are submitted in writing to this box', it asks whether that box exists and whether the crew is aware of it. That is, while Part I is accepted background information, not a fact that needs to be verified, Part II is a directly falsifiable claim — either it is confirmed or it collapses. This asymmetry is why PSC inspectors spend almost all MLC inspection energy looking for the actual onboard equivalent of Part II.

PSC denetimi tek tip değildir; bir piram: PSC supervision is not uniform; it deepens like a pyramid. Initial inspection checks the validity of certificates, the general condition of the ship and the basic compliance of the crew; most inspections start and end here. However, if the inspector detects 'clear grounds' (concrete findings that justify a deeper inspection - for example, missing certificate, damaged equipment, uninformed crew), he moves on to a more detailed inspection and systematically inspects the ship. Expanded inspection is mandatory for high-risk types such as tankers, passenger ships and bulk carriers, as well as high-risk ships; This covers a wide scope, from structural areas to operational systems. An audit is not just a document review: operational checks such as fire and lifesaving drills, rudder testing and emergency generator start-up can also be carried out.

PSC müfettişi, gemiye çıkışından itibare: The PSC inspector requests certificates, security documents and important records from the captain and senior officer upon boarding the ship. In accordance with Regulation 34 of SOLAS Chapter V, the navigation plan must be prepared for each voyage and be accessible on the bridge. The audit takes place in two stages: in the first stage, certificates and documents are checked (document audit); In the second stage, physical equipment, procedures and records are examined (detailed audit). According to the Paris MOU criteria, ships with a high risk profile — based on flag, classification history and number of previous detentions — are subject to more frequent and more comprehensive inspections. Deficiencies are recorded as 'deficiency'; Deficiencies that exceed certain thresholds or are critical for safety will result in detention.

In addition, it is required to have a pilot board plan, emergency cast off procedure and contingency plan. The inspector may ask the officer on the bridge to point out the dangers on his route, explain the rationale for a safe speed, and explain the passage plan approval process.

PSC ve bayrak devleti denetimi, uyumu te: PSC and flag state inspection verify compliance not by a single method but by multiple complementary techniques. The classic method is fuel sample analysis: the MARPOL representative sample is sealed on receipt and, in case of doubt, the sulfur content is measured in the laboratory; In addition, the inspector can also compare the in-use and onboard samples on the ship. Beyond this, remote detection technologies at sea have become increasingly common: some port authorities and research institutions estimate instantaneous sulfur content from the SO₂/CO₂ ratio by sampling the exhaust gas from the ship's smokestack with sniffer drones; This method allows scanning without stopping the ship. Additionally, satellite-based remote sensing can flag suspicious vessels by monitoring plume density over large sea areas, and these findings can be directed to targeted PSC inspections or sample requests. This layered approach combines the broad coverage provided by remote scanning with the precision provided by a physical sample.

PSC'nin yaptırım gücü kademeli ama ağırd: The enforcement power of the PSC is gradual but severe. Detention causes direct commercial loss to the ship and lasts until the deficiencies are corrected and the costs (including additional inspection) are covered. Repeated detentions lead to a regional ban/refusal of access; For example, in the Paris MoU, after a certain number of detentions, the ship is not allowed into the region for increasingly longer periods of time, or even permanently. The consequences are not limited to single ships: detention rates determine the White/Grey/Black list ranking of flag states, which affects the inspection frequency and risk profile of all ships of that flag. Likewise, the performance of classification societies (RO) is also monitored. PSC thus creates systemic quality pressure at flag and class level that goes beyond a single inspection; Substandard management also becomes commercially unsustainable.

Deviation is caused by the local magnetic field created by the ship's own steel and electrical equipment; Therefore, it is specific to the ship and varies depending on the heading of the ship. Deviation values measured at each bow for each ship are kept on a deviation card/table. The full conversion chain is: Compass Course → (deviation applied) → Magnetic Course → (variation applied) → True Course. The algebraic sum of variation and deviation gives the total compass error. Sign convention: east (E) values are positive, west (W) values are negative.

Coefficients B and C are corrected by permanent magnets, coefficient D by soft iron spheres on the sides (quadrantal spheres), and vertical induced magnetism by Flinders bar. Heeling magnet is used for yaw error. The remaining deviation is measured by rotating the ship in all directions (swinging ship) and recorded on the deviation card.

Radar (Radio Detection and Ranging), ele: Radar (Radio Detection and Ranging) is the primary collision avoidance and navigation device that determines the distance and bearing of surrounding ships, land and buoys by emitting electromagnetic pulses and measuring the reflections from targets. Target tracking, CPA/TCPA calculation and maneuver evaluation are performed with ARPA (Automatic Radar Plotting Aid). This section; It covers radar physics (pulse, frequency band, antenna), X-band and S-band difference, ARPA tracking and collision avoidance use, sea/rain clutter and interpretation errors, SOLAS equipment requirements and maintenance/malfunction in engineering depth.
Radar (Radio Detection And Ranging), mik:
Radar (Radio Detection And Ranging) is an active detection system that emits electromagnetic energy pulses in the microwave band (typically 3 GHz / S-band or 9 GHz / X-band) in the direction of the target and extracts the distance, bearing and movement information of the target by analyzing the reflected signal. Marine radar operates regardless of visibility; It can detect targets even in fog, rain, darkness or heavy sea spray conditions.

Maritime radar is the most critical electronic tool of the bridge. Under COLREG Rules 5 and 7, the use of radar is required for proper lookout and conflict risk assessment. SOLAS Chapter V requires ships of 500 GT and above to have at least two independent radars. Modern ARPA (Automatic Radar Plotting Aid) systems automatically track targets, calculate CPA and TCPA and generate alarms on the risk of conflict.
Radar ±1 mm ile en hassastır; float ±5 m: Radar is most sensitive at ±1 mm; float accuracy ±5 mm, capacitive/ultrasonic ±3 mm, hydrostatic ±10 mm accuracy.
Radar anteni kısa süreli güçlü elektroma: The radar antenna sends short-term strong electromagnetic pulses and then goes into reception mode for a short time. This send–listen cycle is repeated hundreds of times per second. The distance to the target is calculated by measuring the time it takes for the sent pulse to hit a target and return (two-way travel time, t).

Radar mevki tayini (Radar Fixing), kıyı:
Radar fixing is the process of determining the exact location of the ship on the map using radar distances and bearings taken from the coastline or significant objects. In situations where GPS access is not available or is questioned, radar fix provides an independent and reliable position source. Radar locator is also used to verify GPS location.

The main advantage of fixing with radar is that it is based on real-world reference: radar detects physical objects in real time and is not dependent on GPS or map databases. Therefore, electronic map errors or GPS distortions do not negatively affect the radar fix. However, radar measurements also have their own systematic and random errors; It is the navigator's responsibility to understand and minimize these errors.

Radar paralel indeksi, köprüüstü seyir t:
Radar parallel index is one of the most practical and important applications of bridge navigation techniques. The basic idea is simple: a line is drawn on the radar screen representing the horizontal distance of a fixed reference point to the ship, and the ship tracks its position relative to this line throughout its course. As long as the reflection of the reference point on the radar screen remains above this line, the ship is on the correct course at the correct distance; Any deviation is immediately noticed visually.

Radar PI is the routine navigational monitoring tool of the bridge during coastal navigation, narrow strait crossings, port approaches and in limited visibility conditions. STCW qualification standards expect officers to have the ability to establish and interpret radar PI; MCA and IMO guidelines define this technique as an integral part of passage plan preparation.

Record of Equipment (Form E), sertifikan: Record of Equipment (Form E) is not a frozen list at the time the certificate is issued, but a living document that must be updated simultaneously with the ship's equipment. Whenever a liferaft is replaced, a fire extinguishing system is replaced or a navigational device is replaced by a different model, this change must be recorded on Form E and, if necessary, undergo class/flag approval. The consequence of this omission is not a mere bureaucratic shortcoming: when the auditor cannot find equipment on Form E that is actually on board the ship, or fails to see an item listed on Form E on the ship, this discrepancy is recorded as a PSC finding in itself, because the accuracy of this list is precisely what the certificate assures. In practice, this means that equipment procurement and maintenance processes require close coordination between the technical department and the documentation process; If a spare part or equipment replacement is recorded in the purchase record but not reflected in Form E, a silently widening gap arises between the certificate and the actual situation, which often emerges at the most crucial moment, during an inspection or accident.

Rhumb line veya loxodrom, tüm meridyenle:
Rhumb line or loxodrome is the surface curve that intersects all meridians at a constant angle. In other words, if the ship always sails at the same angle (true course) to the north-south meridians, the line it follows is loxodrome. The practical consequence of this technical definition is extremely powerful: there is no need to change the route throughout the journey; The rudder is held steady.

In the Mercator projection, a loxodrome appears as a straight line connecting the start and end point. This feature is one of the main reasons that makes the Mercator chart the standard for sea navigation: it is possible to draw and read the route directly on the chart using a ruler and protractor. This practicality makes the loxodrome the preferred line format for short and medium distance cruising.

However, due to spherical geometry, loxodrome does not show the shortest path between two points. The shortest path is located on the great circle (orthodrome). The difference in distance between two lines can reach significant levels depending on the latitude and distance sailed; Especially in high latitudes and long transatlantic routes, this difference can reach hundreds of nautical miles.
Rhumb line, Mercator’da düz çizgi görünü: Rhumb line appears as a straight line in Mercator; This makes navigating a fixed course practical on the map.

RightShip iki ana metrik üretir. Safety: RightShip produces two main metrics. Safety Score (Qi) is a safety risk score between 0.5 and 5.0; It is calculated by weighting factors such as the ship's accident/incident history, age, flag and class performance, PSC results and operator performance. A high score means low risk, and most tenants set a lower threshold (e.g. 2.5). The second metric is the GHG Rating: it gives an emissions efficiency rating from A to G based on the EVDI derived from the ship's design parameters. Thus, RightShip combines both safety and environmental aspects in a single business decision interface; The GHG Rating creates commercial pressure in line with the IMO's CII regime.
RightShip kuruldu (BHP Billiton, Rio Tin: RightShip established (BHP Billiton, Rio Tinto, Cargill)
RightShip'i SIRE veya PSC ile aynı kateg: A common misconception is to put RightShip in the same category as SIRE or PSC. PSC is a statistical system run by states that monitors minimum compliance with international conventions (SOLAS, MARPOL, MLC); SIRE, on the other hand, is a very in-depth and physical inspection specific to the oil majors' own tanker fleet. RightShip, on the other hand, neither exercises government authority nor conducts physical inspections as standard (physical Dry Bulk Inspection is exceptional and targeted); Its main function is to combine existing data (PSC history, classification records, accident reports) and produce a constantly updated commercial risk score. This difference has tangible consequences: a ship may have a clean record at PSC and valid SIRE approval, but due to a past accident record or poor class performance rating, may have a low RightShip Safety Score and be rejected by bulk charterers. The opposite is also possible: a ship that scores well on RightShip may receive serious operational observations in a current SIRE audit. These three systems are not interchangeable, they are overlapping but independent layers that reflect different time periods (RightShip historical data, SIRE current status, PSC current minimum compliance) and different usage purposes.
RightShip'in gerçek gücü, puanın kendisi: The real power of RightShip is not in the score itself, but in how that score is embedded into the leasing processes of large freight owners. Large grain and mineral traders, mining companies and oil companies set a minimum Qi threshold (often 4 and above, higher for some sensitive cargoes) in their corporate policies and build this threshold into their rental systems as a hard filter. The consequence of this is mechanical: a ship below the threshold cannot even be submitted as an offer to that company's broker, because it is automatically eliminated by the system. This is a different form of exclusion than PSC retention; The ship may not have violated any rules, but its commercial access was blocked by a software threshold. This structure makes RightShip an invisible front door to the charter pool rather than a regulatory agency, forcing shipowners to manage risk knowing that a PSC hold or accident record will leave a mark on the score for a long time.

High temperature and salinity can affect equipment performance and the effectiveness of ballast water treatment systems, so these conditions are also taken into account. Tankers entering the region must ensure that, in addition to standard PSC preparation, the inert gas system, cargo security and environmental equipment are working perfectly; because both PSC and commercial vetting focus on these elements.
Riyadh MoU bölgesinin denetim öncelikler: The most concrete geographical fact that determines the control priorities of the Riyadh MoU region is that almost all maritime traffic leaving the Persian Gulf has to pass through the narrow and shallow waters of the Strait of Hormuz. Considering that world crude oil trade and a significant volume of LNG pass through this corridor, both the environmental and geopolitical consequences of a single accident or pollution event would be large-scale. The audit focus of the Riyadh MoU therefore gives disproportionate weight to tanker safety and pollution prevention beyond the scope of the general PSC: inert gas systems, cargo tank safety equipment, oil-water separators and ballast water management are items specifically questioned in routine inspections. The narrow passage corridor of the Bosphorus and heavy tanker traffic also require strict supervision of navigational safety and bridge procedures; Any deficiency affecting a tanker's maneuverability or navigational equipment carries a disproportionate risk in these narrow waterways. As a result, PSC preparation for tankers and LNG ships entering the region should be more comprehensive and cargo/environment-oriented than for other ship types.

The region is a strategic corridor through which a significant part of the world's oil traffic passes; therefore the MoU focuses specifically on oil and chemical tankers. Although it is a relatively new and smaller organization compared to other major MoUs, it enforces auditing standards in line with the IMO PSC Guidelines (Res. A.1138(31)) and provides regional data sharing.

To close this gap, the MoU makes extensive use of IMO's technical cooperation programmes: auditor training, adoption of common audit guidelines and full compliance with the IMO PSC Guidelines (Res. A.1138(31)) are central to this effort. At the same time, the Riyadh MoU seeks to gradually harmonize its regional information system and deficiency/withholding criteria with the more established practices of the Paris and Tokyo MoU; This ensures that inspection results are internationally comparable and makes it easier for ships calling in the region to be prepared to a single consistent standard. The relatively small number of members can actually turn out to be an advantage: the adoption of new practices and common guidelines can be relatively rapid compared to larger and dispersed MoUs. Over time, this harmonization aims to achieve a control capacity appropriate to the strategic importance of the region.

RO'ya devredilen sörvey ve sertifikasyon: The survey and certification authority delegated to the RO does not relieve the flag state of its responsibility; It is only the actual performance of the work that is delegated, with ultimate accountability always remaining with the flag state. When an RO issues a certificate on behalf of a flag state, this certificate legally has the signature of the flag state on the back; When faulty or lax surveying by the RO leads to PSC retention or an accident, the problem does not remain a single RO incident, but is reflected in the IMSAS audit and overall performance report of the flag state authorizing that RO. Flag states must therefore manage their relationship with their ROs not as a one-way delegation of authority but as an agency relationship that must be constantly monitored: this includes regularly reviewing RO performance data (detection rates, delays, recurring deficiencies), conducting annual evaluations, and, where necessary, limiting or completely withdrawing an RO's authority for certain types of certificates or geographical areas. RO Code establishes this control relationship as bilateral accountability: RO is accountable to the flag state, and the flag state is accountable to IMO. In practice, this means that a well-managed flag actually audits its ROs, while a poorly managed flag leaves certification entirely to the RO and does no verification itself; the latter case sooner or later becomes visible in IMSAS and therefore in PSC statistics.

Rota ölçümü ile birlikte sıkça kullanıla: One of the concepts frequently used with route measurement is counter route. Countercourse of a route means following the same line in the opposite direction and is found by adding or subtracting 180° to the actual route value.
Rota ölçümü, deniz haritası üzerinde bel: Course measurement is the process of finding the angular value of the direction between two points determined on the sea chart, relative to true north. This process is the concrete equivalent of the concept of direction in navigation on the map and is mandatory for all speed-time-distance calculations to be applied in a correct direction. Route measurement is not just reading an angle; The projection of the map, the meridian structure and the correct reference of the measurement tool used are integral parts of this process.
Rota ölçümü, denizcilikte en temel işlem: Although route measurement seems to be one of the most basic operations in maritime, it is one of the most error-prone issues. Incorrect reference line, angle reading in the wrong direction, or using the wrong scale map can invalidate the entire navigation plan. Therefore, route measurement is not a mechanical ruler movement; It should be considered as a conscious process in which the concept of direction, map structure and mathematical discipline are applied together.
Rota ölçümü, mesafe ölçümü, ölü hesap me: Route measurement, distance measurement, dead reckoning position advancement, bearing intersection and all classical navigation calculations made on the map work with the Mercator projection assumption. Without this projection, no direct relationship could be established between the straight line on the map and the course taken at sea.
Rota ölçümünde harita projeksiyonunun et: The effect of map projection should also be taken into account in route measurement. In the Mercator projection, directions appear as straight lines; This is a huge advantage for fixed route navigation. However, as the distance between meridians increases at high latitudes, measurement accuracy may decrease. In these regions, route measurement should be done more carefully and, if possible, larger scale maps should be preferred.
Rota ölçümünün her zaman uygun ölçekli h: Route measurement should always be done on a map of appropriate scale. The route measured on a small-scale map may be sufficient for general navigation; However, this route should not be used in narrow waters and port approaches without using large-scale maps. The same route line may overlap shoals or obstacles on the large-scale map.
Rota ölçümünün temel mantığı, ölçülecek: The basic logic of route measurement is based on finding the clockwise angle between the route line to be measured and a meridian direction. This angle is expressed between 0° and 360°. The reference line used during measurement must be a meridian; Parallel lines or the map edge can be used as a reference only as long as they are parallel to the meridian direction.

Running Fix yöntemi, aynı sabit objeye f: The Running Fix method is based on finding the location by advancing the bearings taken at different times on the same fixed object using the course and speed of the ship and intersecting the LOPs obtained from these bearings. It is especially used when there is only one suitable object.
Running fix, açık denizde pratik ve işle: Running fix is practical and functional in the open sea; However, if there is a change in route or speed or if DR discipline is poor, the result is not considered reliable. For this reason, the method is not used instead of fixes obtained with simultaneous LOPs whenever possible.
Running fix, akıntı ve rüzgâr etkilerini: Running fix does not take into account current and wind effects. Therefore, the obtained position may deviate from the real position. It should be combined with the EP (Estimated Position) approach in flowing waters.
Running fix, aynı hedefe farklı zamanlar: Running fix is obtained by evaluating two bearings taken at different times to the same target. When the first bearing is taken, the ship's position is on this line, but its exact location is uncertain. When the second bearing is taken after the ship moves, the first bearing is advanced according to the distance and route traveled by the ship. The intersection of this advanced LOP and the second LOP is the running fix.
Running Fix, aynı sabit objeden farklı z: Running Fix is the assignment of position by transferring two or more bearings taken from the same fixed object at different times, taking into account the progress of the ship. It is the basic fix method used in classical (terrestrial) navigation when a single object is present.
Running fix, göksel seyirde **aynı anda: Running fix is based on the principle of moving **position lines (LOP)** that cannot be obtained at the same time** to the same time**, taking into account the movement of the ship in celestial navigation. Observations made at different times are combined into a single time plane to obtain a fix. It is a practical solution when the number of celestial objects is limited or simultaneous observation is not possible due to weather conditions.
Running Fix, tek bir sabit objeden farkl: Running Fix is a method of determining the position by moving two (or more) LOPs taken at different times from a single fixed object as far as the ship's course and the distance traveled. It is one of the basic solutions of classical navigation, especially in coastal areas with a single object and when visibility is limited.
Running fix, tek NAVAID ile iki kerteriz: Running fix determines position using two bearings with a single NAVAID.
Running fix, yalnızca tek bir seyir yard: Running fix is the determination of position using two bearings taken at different times when only a single navigation aid (NAVAID) is visible. According to Bowditch, this method is based on advancing the first bearing line (LOP) as much as the movement of the ship and intersecting it with the second bearing. It is a critical technique when a single lighthouse is visible offshore or when cruising along the coast.

Rüzgâr, gemi üzerinde iki temel hidrodin:
Wind creates two basic hydrodynamic effects on the ship: drag force and lift force. The combination of these two forces affects the course, speed and maneuverability of the ship at sea. Wind effect should be considered as a critical variable both in offshore navigation planning and during maneuvers in ports.

The effect of wind on the ship depends on the ship's freeboard height (side surface area above the water), superstructure shape and loading condition. In the empty ship (ballast) condition, the wind effect is much more pronounced since the freeboard is high; Since the waterline is high and the freeboard is low on a loaded ship, the wind effect is relatively reduced.

Safety Construction Certificate – İnşa E: Safety Construction Certificate – Construction Safety Certificate
Safety Construction Certificate, bir gem: The Safety Construction Certificate certifies that a ship's structural and mechanical foundation complies with SOLAS Chapter II-1 (structure, compartmentation, stability, machinery, electrical) and II-2 (fire integrity) requirements. While other SOLAS certifications address equipment and operation, this certification ensures the 'skeleton' of the ship: covering the strength of the hull, watertight compartmentation, damage stability and structural bulkheads that limit the spread of fire. It is usually issued by the classification society on behalf of the flag state (as RO) because the issues evaluated directly overlap with the structural expertise of the classification.
Safety Construction Certificate, geminin: The Safety Construction Certificate reflects the approved structural condition of the ship at the time of construction or the last major renovation; Any significant intervention that changes this situation undermines the foundation on which the certificate is based. Structural changes, such as adding a new cabin block to the ship's upper deck, converting an existing open space into a closed volume, or relocating a watertight partition, directly affect the ship's subdivision scheme, damage stability calculations, fire partition plan or total weight distribution. Prior approval of the class and flag state must be obtained before such an intervention is carried out; After approval, a survey is conducted to verify that the change actually meets the requirements of SOLAS Chapter II-1/II-2, and the certificate is reconfirmed or updated according to the results of this survey. A 'silent' modification before this process is completed effectively invalidates the certificate; because the document no longer accurately reflects the actual structural condition of the ship. PSC inspectors look for signs of unauthorized modification, especially on older ships, by comparing the plan information in the certificate with the physical arrangement they observe on the ship; Such non-compliance is recorded as a serious deficiency.
Safety Construction Certificate'ın kapsa: The most critical issue covered by the Safety Construction Certificate is the ship's ability to survive damage. Watertight bulkheads divide the ship into compartments and ensure that the ship remains buoyant and stable when one or more compartments take on water; Damage stability calculations must prove that the ship will remain without sinking or overturning in certain damage scenarios. Watertight doors, bulkhead penetrations and bilge wells maintain this integrity; The approved stability information booklet shows in which loading situations the ship will remain safely balanced and is kept on board. The double bottom and reinforced structural members prevent a single damage from sinking the entire ship in a domino effect. Since these requirements directly coincide with the structural expertise of the classification society, the certificate is usually issued by the classification society on behalf of the flag.

The line between the scope of the Safety Construction Certificate and the scope of the Safety Equipment Certificate and SMC reflects the basic logic of maritime certification architecture: the ship's fixed, permanent 'hardware' and its mobile/replaceable equipment and management systems are secured by separate documents. The Safety Construction Certificate covers the physical framework and permanently installed systems of the ship, such as the hull, bulkheads, main machinery, electrical distribution and fire compartments; These are elements that are difficult to change, expensive and require structural approval. The Safety Equipment Certificate covers portable or replaceable equipment such as life rafts, fire extinguishers and navigational devices; these have more frequent service, replacement and renewal cycles. SMC, on the other hand, secures not any physical equipment, but how this equipment is managed, with what procedures it is operated, and how the crew implements these procedures. This tripartite division is not arbitrary: each requires different inspection expertise (structural engineering, equipment standards, management system inspection) and a different renewal/service rhythm; Combining them into a single certificate would not only complicate the audit process, but also cause a change in one area (e.g. a refit) to unnecessarily reopen other areas (structural approval).

This list records each item of lifesaving, fire and navigational equipment on the ship, one by one, with its number: how many lifeboats and rafts, how many life jackets and diving suits, which fire extinguishing systems, which navigational devices (radar, ECDIS, AIS, VDR) are present. During the inspection, the actual equipment on the ship is expected to match this list exactly; Missing or unlisted equipment is a direct PSC finding. Form E must be updated whenever equipment is changed. This structure ensures that the certificate is not just a 'stamp of compliance' but an auditable record of the ship's safety inventory.

Safety Radio Certificate, bir geminin te: The Safety Radio Certificate certifies that a ship's radio equipment complies with the requirements of SOLAS Chapter IV and GMDSS (Global Maritime Distress and Safety System). The basic idea of GMDSS is to guarantee that a ship's distress call reaches the relevant rescue centers automatically and under all circumstances. Equipment requirements are determined by the sea area in which the ship sails: in A1 near the coast, VHF DSC is sufficient, while A3/A4 ships sailing in the open ocean must also carry HF or satellite (Inmarsat) systems. Thus, each ship has the minimum equipment to call for help from its location.
Safety Radio Certificate'ın temel mantığ: The basic logic of the Safety Radio Certificate is to determine the ship's radio equipment according to the sea area in which it sails; Because the system through which the distress call can be transmitted depends on its location. A1 is coastal waters within range of a VHF DSC coast station and VHF DSC is sufficient. A2 adds the range of an MF DSC station. A3 covers the high seas under satellite (Inmarsat) or HF coverage, A4 covers polar regions outside satellite coverage and requires HF DSC. Each area creates a layered structure by adding new equipment to the previous one. Mandatory GMDSS equipment; Includes VHF/MF/HF DSC, Inmarsat-C, EPIRB, SART/AIS-SART, NAVTEX and security message receivers. The Record of Equipment (Form R) documents this equipment one by one and is compared with the actual situation on board during the inspection.
